These artists share geographic and cultural ties to the region. They use its visual language to explore domesticity, sexuality, women’s work, and the nuances of cultural pride and shame. Pennsylvania Dutch interiors For Buckwalter and Suss, Pennsylvania Dutch aesthetics are intrinsically tied to the home and childhood memory. Both artists paint interior domestic scenes with a flattened, warped perspective. In these spaces, they depict folk objects or family heirlooms that suggest memory, lineage, and loss. “I pull a lot of things directly from my childhood home,” said Buckwalter, who will open “ Heirloom ,” a major institutional solo show at the Allentown Art Museum, on November 21st. An in-progress painting features a chair from her childhood home. Suss, whose solo exhibition “ Night House ” is on view at Jack Shainman , New York, through October 31st, grew up just north of Philadelphia. She began painting interiors after her paternal grandfather died in 2011. Both grandparents had played a major role in her life, and she felt strange among their furniture after they were gone. Their Long Island ranch house was eventually sold and demolished, and Suss inherited its contents. Her earliest paintings offered remembrances of this space and functioned as “part set painting, like a stage backdrop, and part archive of these items.” Night House (Kitchen), 2026 Becky Suss Jack Shainman Gallery Quilt Study (Lone Star), 2025 Anne Buckwalter Uffner & Liu Eventually, Suss began exploring the other side of her family tree. She imagined spaces and objects linked to her mother’s relatives, Irish American on one side and Pennsylvania German on the other. Most of them had died before she was born. “My great-aunt, one of the remaining people in my mother’s family by the time I was alive, had a beautiful chest that was painted. It always seemed like this amazing magical item in her house,” she said. She also recalls childhood visits to the Philadelphia Museum of Art (PMA) and the Barnes Foundation with her mother, a docent. She was drawn to the work of self-taught artists including Henri Rousseau , Horace Pippin , and the Pennsylvania Dutch. In one of her paintings currently on view, titled Living Room (2026), three Pennsylvania Dutch plates from the PMA’s collection are displayed over a bookshelf. McEneaney has lived in Philadelphia since moving there for college in 1973. She paints with a similarly flattened perspective, shaped by Philadelphia museum collections and artists with regional ties. “I feel affinity with vernacular artists like Horace Pippin in terms of subject matter and flatness,” she said. For Suss, however, painting domestic interiors pushes her beyond memory and into a space of desire and imagination. “There’s the idea of coveting things that I can never afford, which is always an element of my work,” she said. “The Pennsylvania Dutch have always been a part of that. There are things that I always just really, really loved.” Samantha Joy Groff’s Mennonite influences Samantha Joy Groff was raised in a Mennonite community in rural Pennsylvania. She paints moody, night-lit scenes of young women in satin negligees who commune with animals in the woods. Her models are often women she knows, and she sometimes depicts them wearing the traditional head coverings common to more conservative Pennsylvania Dutch communities. Groff, who still lives and teaches in the region, says the culture was embedded in her childhood and her design sense. “I grew up going to quilt circles with my Grams and seeing the ornate textiles made by many women in the community; there is a great reverence for what’s called traditional folk arts like quilting, Fraktur, embroidery, and furniture making,” she said. She no longer relies on overt references in her paintings, but she sees the culture in her process: “The staging, working with many women with similar upbringings, drawing, making studies, and then finally painting harkens to the hand-stitched 10-foot quilts my family made,” she said. The patterns, too, carry meaning. “Interlocking circles for weddings, hex signs on barns for luck and prosperity. At first glance, it could be just a design, but like flowers in Victorian paintings, it holds more meaning,” she said. Stars symbolize good luck. Stylized birds, called distelfinks, symbolize happiness. Oaks and acorns bring strength. She’s also a fan of Buckwalter’s work, which makes her feel like she’s “sneaking around my Grams’s house.” Women’s stories and an overlooked heritage Buckwalter describes herself as a homebody who’s very sensitive to space. “I take a lot of pride and joy in making a space feel like home, and nesting, and tidying things,” she said. Part of her interest in Pennsylvania Dutch culture is rooted in the idea of elevating the everyday: Women decorated mundane objects, like chairs and pitchers and bread boxes, with such intricate, frilly designs that they became, in Buckwalter’s words “almost holy.” “There’s something worshipful about domestic space that I really love and that I carry through my work.” Her forthcoming museum show draws directly on that tradition. Working with the museum’s curator, she selected pieces from the Allentown collection, including show towels, embroidered samplers that Pennsylvania Dutch girls, usually 12 or 13 years old, made to prove their readiness for marriage. “It’s basically an embroidered sampler saying, ‘Look, I can sew, I’ll be a good wife,’” she explained. Suss, meanwhile, sees her relationship to the home as part of a multigenerational tradition of housekeeping. Her 2017 solo show “Homemaker” at Jack Shainman included paintings of inherited needlepoints. “My real legacy is homemaking,” she said. “Yet we have five generations of homemakers, and nobody talks about it.” She hopes her paintings in some way elevate this devalued legacy. “Craft is in most cases devalued in comparison to art, because it has utility, which devalues something,” she said. Groff, whose family settled in Pennsylvania in 1696, sees women as the keepers of that tradition. “Women are the great artists in the culture, and rather than just making homes, they are in charge of passing down over 200 years of traditional making that makes their craft so recognizable,” she said. Like Suss, she thinks the word “homemaking” undersells it. “I think ‘homemaking’ dampens the importance of the work. Reframing it as tradition, history, and generational knowledge honors the difficulty and hard work that’s embedded in each piece.” Groff also pushes back on a romantic view of the work. “In our current cultural climate, homemaking is often seen as staying home and making bread as a kind of class fantasy, but in these spaces, my grandma and cousins still have to milk cows on the farm alongside the men,” she said. Like Buckwalter, she sees self-determination at the center of the culture. “I think they are turning ordinary spaces into places of beauty through their individual creative expression.” Groff has carried some of that making into new work, including the garments, from headdresses to props, she created for her show “Huntress.” Artist Rebecca Morgan, who is best known for hyper-detailed, humorous paintings and ceramics about rural Appalachian life and stereotypes, has also embraced Pennsylvania Dutch aesthetics as an emblem of local pride. Growing up in rural Pennsylvania, she often saw hex signs decorating local houses, barns, and sheds. “I always knew them as a ‘Pennsylvania Charm’ to give good luck, or to protect,” she said. “As a child, seeing a hex sign felt specific to my region of Pennsylvania. You didn’t see them in any other scenario other than the Pennsylvania radius, so it was a symbolic emblem of home.” A decade ago, the artist created a series of paintings with the motif. One work, a self-portrait she calls Pennsylvania Princess (year), features the artist wearing a mountain-laurel crown (Pennsylvania’s state flower) and a chest plate featuring a family hex sign that suggests a crest or superhero emblem. “I have always kept this unfinished painting with me because of its sincerity,” she said. A new body of her work is currently on view in “ Painting in the Apocalypse ” at Asya Geisberg . Contemporary ambiguity meets Pennsylvania Dutch styles While the culture of the Pennsylvania Dutch, with its emphasis on family, faith, and homemaking, offers a traditional, even conservative framework for living, contemporary artists are using the style to create more nuanced, ambiguous spaces. Groff, for her part, says the eroticism in her work runs counter to her upbringing. “When you grow up in a community like this, although known for its warm and friendly people, there is very little emotional excess,” she said. “‘Rural stoicism’ comes into play. But the emotional restraint I felt and continue to feel made everything bubbling inside of me that was messy want to seep out.” The artist places her figures in remote settings, “away from the metaphorical community spaces where the emotional excess spills out through the figuration—a more psychological space, where danger lurks just outside the picture plane.” Her works have also been heavily influenced by her research into braucherei , a Pennsylvania Dutch religious folk healing practice. “I wanted to make paintings that evoke the divine in a way that may only make sense to a few,” she said. “Even the [Pennsylvania] Dutch tradition of hex signs on barns, which is debated as decorative or symbolic, informs how I make paintings that connect to a religious experience.” The scenes teeter between a kind of ecstatic spirituality and heightened sexuality, where no truth is discernibly clear. Counter View, 2025 Sarah McEneaney Taymour Grahne Projects Still Life with Ankle Cuffs, 2026 Anne Buckwalter New Discretions Buckwalter acknowledges that Pennsylvania Dutch culture “very much amplifies heteronormative values” and explains that she was raised in a strict Christian household where there was a “moral panic” over sexuality and the possibility of premarital sex. She describes herself as a bisexual, queer woman who is “happily and intentionally childless.” But she says she maintains “a lot of affection and warmth for my upbringing, even the strict religious parts.” In her paintings, sexuality and kink live comfortably within these idyllic, old-fashioned worlds. “I think one way that my work functions is as a way of reconciling or marrying these disparate parts of myself, and I’m kind of making the statement that all these things can live together even though they seem like they conflict with each other,” she said. For Suss, tension and ambiguity function more subtly. The artist leaves figures out of her spaces entirely. The interiors lack any markers of a particular time. Such distortions enhance her storytelling. “I wanted to leave the paintings open to be the backdrop to your life or my life or whoever’s life,” she said. “When you depart from a memory, the departures from truth tell the story.”

title: What Sold at Frieze London and Frieze Masters 2026
summary: Frieze London and Frieze Masters wrapped up their 2026 editions on Sunday, October 18th, capping off a lively week of art in the British capital. It was a bumper Frieze Week for London’s art scene, with some eight satellite fairs orbiting the main events, alongside a standout slate of gallery and museum exhibitions. Held in Regent’s Park from October 14th through 18th, Frieze’s fairs drew 95,000 visitors from 108 countries and regions, including representatives from a record 426 institutions. International attendance was particularly encouraging: Visitor numbers from India and China more than doubled year over year, while the fairs also reported growing attendance from North America, Europe, and the Middle East. The famous faces were out in force, too. Among those spotted weaving through the aisles were Madonna, Pedro Pascal, Daniel Craig, Tilda Swinton, Andrew Garfield, and Helena Bonham Carter. But beyond the celebrity sightings and social gatherings, the week offered encouraging evidence of collectors’ willingness to spend. The top reported transaction was Jan Brueghel the Elder ’s Still Life of Flowers in a Stoneware Vase (ca. 1607–08), sold by Hauser & Wirth at Frieze Masters for around £5 million ($6.64 million). Meanwhile, several booths across Frieze London’s emerging-gallery sections sold out within hours of opening. Institutional collecting was another defining feature. The Frieze Tate Fund acquired works by Artsy Vanguard alum Michaela Yearwood-Dan from Hauser & Wirth and Luis Fernando Zapata from a joint presentation by Galería Elvira Moreno and Alonso Garcés Galería. The Whitworth acquired works from Sadie Coles HQ, Sprüth Magers , and Proyectos Ultravioleta, while the Arts Council Collection acquired works from Arcadia Missa, Galeria Wschód, Union Pacific, and Phillida Reid. Meanwhile, works presented by Albarrán Bourdais and Ames Yavuz were acquired for the V&A, and Abbot Hall acquired works by Okiki Akinfe from Ginny on Frederick. Ella Fleck, presented by Ehrlich Steinberg, received the Camden Art Centre Emerging Artist Award, while Unathi Mkonto , presented by Goodman Gallery —one of Artsy’s best booths from the fair —won the Nicoletta Fiorucci Foundation Prize. As London-based art advisor Daniel Malarkey noted, “at Frieze, what happens between the aisles is as important as the sales,” he told Artsy. “I run into London-based artists—we have some of the best emerging and established artists in the world—collectors, museum curators; new projects happen mid-conversation.” He added that his clients were buying and they added their names to several waiting lists for coveted works. With Art Basel Paris poised to command the market’s uppermost price brackets, Frieze’s strength may lie in allowing collectors a little more variety. Its range of prices, generations, and artistic practices creates space for acquisitions driven as much by curiosity and conviction as by market momentum. Or, as Malarkey put it: “Frieze is cool again.” Here, we round up the key sales reported by galleries across Frieze London and Frieze Masters 2026. Top sales at Frieze London and Frieze Masters 2026 In addition to the leading Brueghel sale, other reported sales across the two fairs at Hauser & Wirth included: Francis Picabia ’s Untitled (ca. 1941–43) for €1.1 million ($1.24 million). Pablo Picasso ’s Violon (Violin) (1943) for €850,000 ($955,000). Picabia’s Transparence, visage de femme (Transparency, Face of a Woman) (ca. 1928–29) for a high six-figure price. Avery Singer ’s Solver (v.3) (2026) for $800,000 and George Condo ’s Figure Composition (2026) for $600,000. Other transactions included: Lee Bul ’s Perdu—Silhouette VII (2026) for $290,000. Christina Kimeze ’s Game on (crane’s cut) (2026) for $195,000. Allison Katz ’s Lip Service (2026) for $195,000. Anj Smith ’s Required Reading (2026) for $195,000. Nicole Eisenman ’s Drawing for The Stack (2022) for $175,000. Eisenman’s Edie (2025) for $150,000. Two works by William Kentridge , Drawing for L’Orfeo (Tree - Cyanide Gold) (2024) and Drawing for L’Orfeo (Vessels in Landscape) (2025), for $150,000 each. Eisenman’s Drawing for Stack (2026) for $75,000. Nathanaëlle Herbelin ’s Elie (2026) for €58,000 ($65,200). Phyllida Barlow ’s Untitled: Les Noces; (towers/grids); 2022 (2022) for $50,000. Glenn Ligon ’s Study for Blue (for JB) #16 (2026) for $25,000. Kimeze’s Exchange (2026) for $14,000. At Frieze Masters, David Zwirner and Victoria Miro jointly presented four paintings by Alice Neel —one of Artsy’s best booths from the fair . All four works sold for between $1.6 million and $1.8 million each, including one acquired by a major museum. At Frieze London, David Zwirner’s sales were led by a new painting by Michaël Borremans for $1.5 million. Other reported transactions included: A new painting by Dana Schutz for $900,000. A new painting by Lisa Yuskavage for $450,000. A new painting by Sasha Gordon for $400,000, acquired by a European museum. A new painting by Portia Zvavahera for $300,000. Two new paintings by Rose Wylie for $200,000 each. A new painting by Yu Nishimura for $170,000, acquired by an Asian museum. A new photograph by Wolfgang Tillmans for $145,000. A new painting by Emma McIntyre for $140,000. A new painting by Louis Fratino for $120,000. A new work on paper by Marcel Dzama for $100,000. A new painting by Walter Price for $30,000. Thaddaeus Ropac reported a series of six-figure sales at Frieze London, led by Martha Jungwirth ’s Untitled (Berggasse 19) (2026) for €560,000 ($629,000). Other sales included: Antony Gormley ’s Aside (2025) for £500,000 ($665,000). Adrian Ghenie ’s Untitled (2026) for €380,000 ($427,000). Leoncillo ’s Mutilazione (1963) for €300,000 ($337,000). Megan Rooney ’s Radio Silence (2026) for £280,000 ($372,000). Joan Snyder ’s Elegy for Souls (2025) for $275,000 and Deep In Me (2025) for $195,000. Two paintings by Denzil Forrester , Professor Version (2025) and Yard (2025), for £175,000 ($233,000) each. A second work by Jungwirth, Untitled (Berggasse 19) (2026), for €180,000 ($202,000). Zadie Xa ’s Omens (2026) for £65,000 ($86,450). Sylvie Fleury ’s Moonwalk (2025) for €65,000 ($73,000). Untitled, 2026 Martha Jungwirth Thaddaeus Ropac At Frieze Masters, Waddington Custot sold Jean Dubuffet ’s Le malentendu 23 décembre 1976 for £950,000 ($1.26 million). The gallery also placed two works by Eduardo Chillida for £280,000 ($372,000) and £140,000 ($186,000), respectively. Xavier Hufkens reported sales at Frieze London led by a historic work on paper by Richard Serra for $750,000. Other transactions included: A suite of works on paper by Louise Bourgeois for $400,000. Two paintings by Lesley Vance for prices ranging from $110,000 to $220,000. A painting by McArthur Binion for $150,000. Three sculptures by Mark Manders for “approximately” €120,000 ($135,000) each. A large painting by Ulala Imai for $125,000. Two neon works by Tracey Emin for prices ranging from £95,000 to £105,000 ($126,350–$139,650) each. A bronze sculpture by Sterling Ruby for $95,000 and a ceramic work for $90,000. A painting by Henry Taylor for $65,000. A small sculpture by Thomas Houseago for $55,000. A painting by Cecilia Vicuña for $50,000. A painting by Cassi Namoda for $18,000. Bastian reported sales at Frieze Masters including Max Pechstein ’s Stillleben mit Pfeife for around €700,000 ($787,000), and Pierre-Auguste Renoir ’s Femme assise dans un paysage for “around” €500,000 ($562,000). The gallery also reported the sale of Renoir’s Paysage (ca. 1897) for “approximately” €300,000 ($337,000). White Cube sold 11 works by Ilana Savdie , including The Harbingers (2026) to a museum for $325,000 and Syncitia No. 2 (2026) for $260,000. Other reported sales included: Gabriel Orozco ’s Lion Fish (2024) for $300,000. Shara Hughes ’s Secret Secret (2026) for $175,000. Isamu Noguchi ’s Kaki-persimmons (1988/2023) for $170,000. title: The Met selects Danh Vo and Sandra Mujinga for 2027 facade and Great Hall commissions.
summary: The Metropolitan Museum of Art has announced its 2027 commissions for the Museum’s Fifth Avenue facade and Great Hall. Danh Vo , who lives and works in Berlin and Mexico City, will create new work for the four niches of the Beaux-Arts facade as the Genesis Facade Commission. These works will be on view September 16, 2027, through June 13, 2028. Inside the museum, artist Sandra Mujinga , who lives and works in Oslo, will present a site-specific installation for the Great Hall, on view November 4, 2027, through April 4, 2028. Vo’s practice draws on found and historical objects, from religious relics and photographs to fragments of antiquity, to examine how power and meaning accrue to things over time. His commission is the eighth in the facade series, following works by Wangechi Mutu , Carol Bove , Hew Locke , Nairy Baghramian , Lee Bul , Jeffrey Gibson , and, this year, Liu Wei . Vo’s commission will be the fourth under the museum’s multiyear partnership with Genesis Art Initiatives. Mujinga works across sculpture, video, sound, and performance, often creating spectral figures that resist fixed identities. Her Great Hall installation—the fourth in that series after Kent Monkman , Jacolby Satterwhite , and Tong Yang-Tze —will consider the politics of being seen and the traces bodies leave behind. “Danh Vo and Sandra Mujinga both treat history as something alive and unsettled and are deeply attuned to the ways objects and bodies carry meaning across time,” said Max Hollein, director of the museum. “Visitors will meet Vo's project on Fifth Avenue and be greeted by Mujinga's as they enter the Great Hall, so that together these commissions frame the very experience of arriving at the museum.” David Breslin, curator of modern and contemporary art, called the pair “two of the most inventive and essential artists of our time.” Vo, born in 1975 in Bà Rịa, Vietnam, represented Denmark at the 2015 Venice Biennale and was the subject of a 2018 survey, “Danh Vo: Take My Breath Away,” at the Guggenheim . Mujinga, born in 1989 in Goma, Democratic Republic of the Congo, has had recent solo shows at Belvedere 21 in Vienna and the Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam , and was included in the 2022 Venice Biennale main exhibition “ The Milk of Dreams .”

title: All the Art You Need to See during Paris Art Week 2026
summary: Like many, I don’t think you ever need an excuse to go to Paris. But with Art Basel Paris returning to the Grand Palais from October 23rd to 25th, there’s an especially good reason to plan a fall escape to the City of Light . Beyond the fair, Paris will be buzzing with satellite fairs, gallery openings, and museum exhibitions that span centuries of art history and the best of contemporary art. It’s an especially exciting time to explore the city’s gallery hubs—namely Matignon Saint-Honoré and the Marais—as well as its institutions, from the storied Musée d’Orsay to the cutting-edge Bourse de Commerce. Here’s our 10-stop guide to making the most of Paris Art Week 2026. All 10 stops are also featured in City Guide , a new feature in the Artsy app that helps you discover art nearby, save the shows, galleries, and fairs you want to see, and build your own art itineraries. 1. Art Basel Paris Oct. 21–25 | Grand Palais | 8th arrondissement The centerpiece of Paris Art Week returns to the majestic Grand Palais for its fifth edition, bringing together more than 200 galleries from 41 countries. In addition to booths from local Parisian heavyweights like Perrotin , Chantal Crousel, and Almine Rech , I’d make a point of exploring Emergence, the sector dedicated to solo presentations by rising artists on the balcony that overlooks the main fair floor. For a more art historical perspective, head to the Premise sector, which features curated presentations like Robert Indiana and Ellsworth Kelly from Olney Gleason and El Anatsui , Uche Okeke , and Obiora Udechukwu from kó . The fair begins with VIP previews on October 21st and 22nd, followed by a ticketed vernissage on the afternoon of the 22nd. Public admission runs October 23rd through 25th. 2. Paris Internationale Oct. 20–24 | 187–189 Quai de Valmy | Canal Saint-Martin One of my favorite counterparts to Art Basel Paris is Paris Internationale, now in its 12th edition. This year the fair moves to a new venue along the Canal Saint-Martin. Known for its independent spirit and lively atmosphere, it’s a great place to discover new artists and galleries. The fair holds an invite-only preview on October 19th, with the main fair running October 20th through 24th. 3. Marais galleries and Post-Fair Various locations | Marais In the Marais, make time for the galleries clustered along rue de Turenne, rue Debelleyme, and the surrounding streets. Four shows that are high on my list: Jordan Casteel at Thaddaeus Ropac : Opening October 19th, “Winter Sun” marks the American artist’s first solo exhibition in France. The show brings together paintings of people, botanicals, and landscapes in a palette drawn from the cool light of winter. Alma Allen at Perrotin: An exhibition of new, large-scale bronzes marks Allen’s first solo exhibition in Paris, and his first with Perrotin, which began representing him earlier this year. It comes ahead of his presentation at the U.S. pavilion at the Venice Biennale. Rosana Paulino at Mendes Wood DM : For her first solo show in Paris, opening October 19th, the Brazilian artist presents new large-scale paintings of female figures in natural settings that explore Black womanhood. Oscar Murillo at David Zwirner : “Unfinished Thinking: Paintings and Social Maps” brings together paintings layered with color and gesture that explore shared experiences, labor, and migration. While in the area, don’t miss Chris Sharp’s Los Angeles–born fair, Post-Fair, which crosses the Atlantic for its first international edition, taking over two buildings at 74 and 79 rue du Temple. More than 30 galleries will present solo and two-artist presentations throughout the open rooms, creating the feel of a sprawling group exhibition rather than a conventional booth fair. Running October 19th to 24th, the fair is free to attend with advance registration. 4. Design Miami Paris Oct. 20–24 | Hôtel de Maisons, 51 rue de l’Université | 7th arrondissement Design Miami Paris returns to the magnificent 18th-century Hôtel de Maisons, once home to Karl Lagerfeld . Expect a striking mix of rare historic and contemporary design, from furniture to sculptural objects. The setting is part of the appeal, including the Design at Large program, which brings larger installations into the courtyard and idyllic gardens. An invitation-only preview takes place on October 20th, followed by public days from October 21st through 24th. 5. Galleries in Matignon Saint-Honoré and the 8th Various locations | 8th arrondissement The Matignon Saint-Honoré Nocturne on October 19th offers a festive kickoff to Paris Art Week. Some 38 galleries in the 8th arrondissement will stay open until 9 p.m., while the main streets are closed to traffic, turning the neighborhood into a lively gallery stroll. It’s an ideal time to explore one of the city’s major gallery districts, with everything from modern masters to contemporary art and design. Three shows worth prioritizing: Alexander Calder at Hauser & Wirth : “François Premier” revisits Calder’s time in France in the 1950s, with mobiles, sculptures, and works on paper. The centerpiece is Les Granettes (1953), a monumental standing mobile which has not been exhibited publicly in 72 years. Lee Krasner at Gagosian : Presented by Gagosian, Olney Gleason, and the Pollock-Krasner Foundation, “Works from the 1960s” marks the first solo presentation in France devoted to the pioneering Abstract Expressionist. The show spotlights a pivotal decade in her career and coincides with the major “Krasner Pollock ” exhibition at the Metropolitan Museum of Art . Tracey Emin at White Cube : The artist’s first solo exhibition at the gallery’s Paris space features new paintings and bronze sculptures, following her acclaimed Tate Modern show. 6. Musée d’Orsay: Jenny Holzer, “J’ai vu” and Mary Cassatt 1 rue de la Légion d’Honneur | 7th arrondissement Jenny Holzer ’s exhibition of text-based work was conceived specifically for and in collaboration with the storied museum. Holzer found inspiration in the museum’s archive, drawing on artists’ letters as well as literature from the period of its holdings, 1848 to 1914. The show features an LED sign stretching through four galleries, along with engraved stone benches and columns. Perhaps most exciting are the light projections on the museum’s iconic exterior facing the Seine, which you can witness from October 18th to 22nd, from dusk to 11 p.m. While you’re there, don’t miss Mary Cassatt ’s retrospective, which brings together nearly 80 paintings, pastels, and prints, tracing the American Impressionist ’s remarkable trajectory and output. 7. Art Basel Paris Public Program Oct. 21–25 | Various locations Some of the week’s most exciting art is temporarily popping up across the city thanks to Art Basel’s public program of installations. A highlight is Kutluğ Ataman ’s celebrated video environment Küba (2005), on view at the Beaux-Arts de Paris and curated by Nathan Ladd. The expansive piece features 40 monitors, each one showing a resident of a since-demolished settlement on the outskirts of Istanbul. Together, their stories form a portrait of community. Elsewhere, look for three monumental bronzes by Tracey Emin at the Parvis des Droits-de-l’Homme, Alice Diop’s Geste de Consolation (presented by Miu Miu) at the Palais d’Iéna, and a herd of plush animals by Cosima von Bonin at the Petit Palais. Monumental sculptures will also line the Avenue Winston Churchill. 8. Fondation Cartier: Ibrahim Mahama, “The Harvest Season” Oct. 22–Feb. 28 | 2 Place du Palais-Royal | 1st arrondissement Ghanaian artist Ibrahim Mahama takes over the Fondation Cartier ’s entire exhibition space, housed in the institution’s new building, which opened last year. The show features site-specific works and previously unseen versions of some of Mahama’s best-known installations. He has also invited nine artists and collectives to show with him, including photographer James Barnor and painter Gideon Appah . Known for transforming discarded materials and archival objects into monumental installations, Mahama explores Ghana’s history of colonization and the global passage of goods. 9. Bourse de Commerce: “Remember Me” Through Jan. 18 | 2 rue de Viarmes | 1st arrondissement The Bourse de Commerce is known for its ambitious exhibitions. This time, photography takes center stage in “Remember Me,” bringing together some 700 works by more than 70 artists from the Pinault Collection, all exploring memory in different ways. Barbara Kruger , whose work gives the exhibition its title, takes over the spectacular rotunda with an installation of text, film, and voices. Meanwhile, Irving Penn gets a gallery of his own, filled with some 450 photographs. 10. The Louvre: Kader Attia and Elizabeth Peyton Through Dec. 14 | Musée du Louvre, rue de Rivoli | 1st arrondissement For the past two years, contemporary artists Kader Attia and Elizabeth Peyton have had studios at the Louvre and made new work while exploring its collections. The results are on view in “Hosts at the Louvre.” Attia presents a film and installation exploring history and the act of looking, while Peyton presents a series of her signature portraits alongside paintings that reinterpret the museum’s masterpieces. While the Louvre is synonymous with art history, it’s an exciting opportunity to see leading contemporary artists connecting the age-old collection with the present.

title: Our 8 Favorite Artworks under $10,000 from the 2026 London Art Fairs
summary: London is in full swing. The streets are buzzing, the galleries are packed, and a small army of art-world insiders is weaving through traffic on Lime bikes, racing between openings, fair booths, and late-night parties. It can only mean one thing: Frieze Week has returned . And this year, the British capital feels particularly alive, with an infectious energy that suggests London is back on form. At the center of the action are Frieze London and Frieze Masters , bringing nearly 300 galleries from around the world to Regent’s Park. But the excitement stretches far beyond the big white tents. Minor Attractions has taken over a Fitzrovia hotel, 1-54 Contemporary African Art Fair has returned to Somerset House, and PAD London is bringing collectible design back to Berkeley Square. Meanwhile, newcomers London Invitational, Paraíso, and Fair Play are adding fresh perspectives to the week’s packed calendar. From Mayfair’s polished galleries to the more experimental corners of the city, everyone’s talking about what they’ve discovered. Amid the blockbuster presentations, seven-figure price tags, and champagne-fueled soirées, however, some of the week’s most compelling artworks come at considerably more approachable prices. Artsy’s editors have been pounding the pavements (and occasionally hopping on a Lime bike themselves) to find the standout works priced under $10,000. Here are our favorites. Frieze London and Frieze Masters Through October 18 Regent’s Park, NW1 4NR The main events of the week. Frieze London and Frieze Masters have once again taken over Regent’s Park, bringing together the biggest names in contemporary art alongside centuries of art history. Josefine Reisch, Tank Louis , 2026 Presented by Galerie Noah Klink at Frieze Price: €3,500 ($3,926) Tank Louis, 2026 Josefine Reisch Galerie Noah Klink The Cartier Tank watch has been worn by everyone from Andy Warhol to Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis—but this design icon has an unlikely military history. Louis Cartier designed it around 1917, reportedly inspired by the Renault tanks of World War I, with its parallel sidebars echoing the vehicles’ treads. More than a century later, it has become a byword for understated luxury. Berlin-based painter Josefine Reisch takes this object as the starting point for her small painting Tank Louis (2026), in her solo booth in the Focus section. There, Galerie Noah Klink has wrapped the walls in industrial silver foil, matching the painting’s background and frame. Reisch breaks the watch down into its constituent parts—face, strap, and underside—each depicted in meticulous detail using oil, acrylics, wax, and metal leaf. The painting is one of several works exploring how military technology meets luxury branding. The booth’s centerpiece is her diptych of a Rolls-Royce aircraft engine from London’s Imperial War Museum. As European governments ramp up defense spending, these intertwined histories of commerce, desire, and violence feel newly urgent. —Josie Thaddeus-Johns, associate director of content Corinna Gosmaro, Piccolo Paesaggio (Lava) , 2026 Presented by Carvalho at Frieze London Price: $7,000 Piccolo Paesaggio (Lava), 2026 Corinna Gosmaro Carvalho Who knew air filters could make for such compelling paintings? Italian artist Corinna Gosmaro paints on sheets of polyester fiber, transforming this everyday, often unseen material into something almost ethereal. Working with spray paint, oil, and graphite, she coaxes color into the stubborn fibers, sometimes using her fingers to work it in. The result is a fascinating play of depth and lightness, as colors appear to sink into the material in some places and hover above it in others. At first glance, her works look entirely abstract, but titles like Piccolo Paesaggio (Lava) (2026) give a gentle nudge to the mind and the eye. I see a thrilling volcanic scene, with flickering flames and inky rock against a pastel-colored sky. It’s an exciting taste of what’s to come from Gosmaro, who will have her first solo show with Carvalho in 2027. —Casey Lesser, director of editorial and content João Artur da Silva, Untitled , 1953 Presented by Perve Galeria at Frieze Masters Price: £6,500 ($8,614) Untitled, 1953 João Artur da Silva Perve Galeria A crumbling brick wall, a shattered egg, a pair of mysterious spheres: there’s plenty to puzzle over in this wonderfully strange little drawing by Portuguese Surrealist João Artur da Silva . The work is presented by Lisbon’s Perve Galeria in the Spotlight section of Frieze Masters dedicated to overlooked figures from the 20th century. Born in 1928, da Silva was a founding member of the Portuguese Surrealist Group in the 1940s, before he moved to Britain in the late 1950s. His experimental practice has spanned painting, drawing, sculpture, and photography, though he is always fascinated by the unexpected possibilities of images. This small, intricate composition captures that spirit beautifully: architectural fragments and everyday objects are thrown together in a strange landscape, composed monochromatically in black ballpoint pen with meticulous precision but little regard for conventional logic. At 98, the artist remains a fascinating and still underappreciated figure in post-war art. More than seven decades after it was made, this curious drawing maintains a capacity to confuse. —Arun Kakar, senior art market editor Minor Attractions Through October 17 50 Newman St, London W1T 3EB The scrappy satellite fair is back for another year, this time across the first-floor rooms of the brand-new Art Deco–inspired hotel The Newman in Fitzrovia. Expect to find artworks everywhere, from the beds and showers to the bathroom sinks. Hannah Tilson, Still Here , 2026 Presented by Cedric Bardawil Price: £2,500 ($3,340) Scottish artist Hannah Tilson creates what she calls “patternscapes.” In this work, layers of fabric in primary colors swirl into a kinetic scene, where a lightly depicted face peeks through the translucent forms. Tilson’s thoughtfully chaotic technique gives the impression of school uniforms, buttons, and shirt collars, without directly depicting any of them. Measuring just 30.5 by 40.5 centimeters, the painting manages to create a tight universe that challenges our perception. While Tilson usually works on paper, this one is one of her latest works on panel. According to gallerist Cedric Bardawil, who has worked with the artist for several years, she also mixes her own paint, designed to ensure its longevity. —J.T.J. PAD London Through October 18 Berkeley Square, Mayfair, W1J 6EN The dazzling design fair returns to Berkeley Square with a thrilling array of objects, from pristine 20th-century furniture by the likes of Finn Juhl and Jean Prouvé to cutting-edge contemporary works by Samuel Ross and Misha Kahn . Diederik Schneemann, Matchbox Mini Clock , 2026 Presented by Rademakers Gallery Price: €5,000 ($5,628) Matchbox Mini Clock, 2026 Diederik Schneemann Rademakers Gallery The Dutch designer Diederik Schneemann has a way with transforming familiar objects. Tucked inside an inventive cabinet made from thrift shop paintings , I discovered his Matchbox Mini Clock (2026), constructed from hundreds of matchbooks collected from restaurants, bars, cafés, and hotels during his travels. There’s something wonderfully nostalgic about the piece, which is fully functional. Matchbooks are hardly a necessity these days, but rather little souvenirs to pocket after dinner or drinks at a favorite spot, and bring home to live alongside your fancy candles. Here, arranged in neat stacks and rows, they become keepsakes of nights out, celebrations, and places visited. What better way to mark the passage of time than with these little repositories of memories? —C.L. 1-54 London Through October 18th Somerset House, Strand, WC2R 1LA Across three wings of Somerset House, this is the best way to experience contemporary art from Africa and its diaspora. The 14th London edition of this international art fair has a particular focus on African modernist artists, responding to increased international attention. Cinthia Sifa Mulanga, As She Abides in a New Plane , 2026 Presented by Gillian Jason Gallery Price: £2,500 ($3,340) As She Abides in a New Plane, 2026 Cinthia Sifa Mulanga Gillian Jason Gallery Almost impossible to capture in still photographs, this sculptural wall work by Cinthia Sifa Mulanga will boggle your mind. Mulanga, who was featured in The Artsy Vanguard 2023–24 , is known for dreamy paintings of Black women in lavish interiors, often playing with perspective through collage and oils. In this small red-toned work, her obsession with corridors, doorways, and architectural spaces becomes even more pointed, quite literally. Made from collage, charcoal, and oil pastel, the work is a fully three-dimensional pyramid depicting a stately hallway that leads to a window overlooking greenery. The vanishing point rises from the canvas and plays a satisfying trick on the eye. Even in this small scale, Mulanga presents a fantastical escape for her subjects, a complex but luxurious vision of Black leisure. —J.T. J. London Invitational Through October 18 30 Grosvenor Square, W1K 9AN A strong contender for the most stylish fair of the week, London Invitational’s debut takes place at the newly opened Chancery Rosewood hotel in Mayfair. With its majestic interiors, hushed luxury, and impeccably presented artworks, the fair feels a world away from the frenzy of Regent’s Park. Dan Attoe, Dark Falls with Lodge , 2026 Presented by Andrew Reed Gallery Price: $6,000 Dark Falls with Lodge, 2026 Dan Attoe Andrew Reed Gallery Miami-based Andrew Reed Gallery presents a small but transporting painting by American artist Dan Attoe , whose atmospheric landscapes often juxtapose natural wonder with a sense of something sinister. Inspired by David Lynch ’s cult classic Twin Peaks , the work depicts a warmly lit lodge perched above a thundering waterfall, enveloped in mist and a wash of deep blues and greens. It could have come straight out of the TV show’s mountainous opening credits. Attoe is known for his meticulous, almost obsessive technique, building up richly detailed scenes that feel familiar and fantastical. Here, his delicate painterly touch gives the tiny canvas a cinematic quality, drawing us into a world that seems to stretch well beyond its edges. In the polished surroundings of the Chancery Rosewood, this little window into the Pacific Northwest is a particularly engrossing find. —A.K. Paraíso Through October 18 35 Marylebone Road, NW1 5LS The surprise hit of the week might just be Paraíso, the new fair dedicated to Latin American art. Bringing together contemporary talent and modern masters from across the region and its diaspora, it brings an adventurous mix of galleries, independent artists, and performances. Nelson Hernández, Argos the Dog , 2026 Presented by Isabel Croxatto Galería Price: $3,800 Argos the Dog, 2026 Nelson Hernández Isabel Croxatto Galería D’oh! Is that Homer Simpson? At Paraíso, Chilean artist Nelson Hernández gives Springfield’s most famous resident an unexpected makeover . Painted in ghostly shades of blue, gray, and white, in a style reminiscent of Gerhard Richter , the familiar cartoon character is turned eerie, his gaping mouth and bulging eyes emerging through a blurred surface. And yes, his head is attached to a dog’s body. Born in Patagonia and now based in London, Hernández has a clever knack for plucking familiar images from popular culture and art history and making them feel wonderfully strange. His practice explores how globalization has flattened cultural identities, mixing high and low references with an irreverent disregard for their original context. Here, the world’s most recognizable cartoon dad becomes something altogether more enigmatic. —A.K.

title: For Collector Irene Panagopoulos, Art Is a Search for Belonging
summary: Irene Y. Panagopoulos’s collecting journey began with a handful of paintings given to her by her father. Today, her collection has grown beyond the walls of her home. “I think my life overflows. I have more art than I can put on all the walls in my house. Collectors always have more than fits anywhere. This is what defines a collector,” she said. Collecting for Panagopoulos is a journey that probes questions of identity, belonging, and the world around her. Shaped by her Greek heritage and an interest in how artists navigate cultural and geographic boundaries, her collection reflects both personal experience and wider social concerns. Now, as she presents works from the collection outside Greece for the first time, she is inviting a new audience into that conversation. The London-born, Greece-based collector is bringing a selection of those works to the Hellenic Centre, marking the collection’s first exhibition outside Greece. Titled “Revisiting: Fernweh, or Nostalgia for Unknown Lands,” the exhibition brings together 17 works spanning the 18th century to the present. Curated by Katerina Hadji, it explores how Greece has been imagined and reimagined through travel, memory, and displacement. Artists in the show include Kader Attia , Vlassis Caniaris , Marc Chagall , Claire Fontaine , Elizabeth Peyton , Sean Scully , and Niki de Saint Phalle . For Panagopoulos, who was born in London to a Greek father and Italian mother, the presentation also marks a personal return to her birthplace. “The exhibition will be a miniature of our collection. It is a concentrated megadose of feelings,” she said. Panagopoulos speaks fondly of the light in Greece. “There’s a certain brightness that is so good for the soul,” she said. London, for all her affection for it, feels dark by comparison. But when asked whether that light influences her collecting, she pointed instead to the realities of living in Greece, including its economic difficulties: “If we live in the same place, we definitely have similar concerns.” A collection shaped by identity Her relationship with art began long before she became a collector. “I came from a home that was filled with original art and designer objects,” she said. She studied art, initially more interested in making it than acquiring it. “I didn’t come out as an art expert or an artist from my studies. I wasn’t planning on becoming a collector either, but I was always interested in art.” Other responsibilities followed. “I was married; I made a family; I entered the family business,” she said. It was only after her children finished school that she returned to her earlier interests. “And that’s when I was able to go back into doing things that gave me pleasure, like visiting museums.” The paintings inherited from her father became the starting point. “Initially, I wanted to complete the puzzle—return some of the missing parts and missing objects,” she recalled. But what began as an attempt to fill gaps soon expanded into something more. By visiting galleries, fairs, and museums, she encountered artists and works that opened up new directions. “I started discovering artists and more amazing works of art. That’s how I began acquiring.” Among her earliest interests were Greek artists who had built careers abroad. “I wanted to put that story in my collection,” she said. She began with Lucas Samaras , drawn to his combination of “a lot of Pop influence” and “the narrative of his own birthplace.” Lynda Benglis , whose work features in the London exhibition, had also impressed Panagopoulos as a student. “I admired her audacity at competing with all the male artists of her generation and making it.” Learning of Benglis’s Greek heritage later prompted her to reconsider the artist’s work. She began to recognize echoes of ancient Greek columns and sculpted female figures, particularly in “how the fabric covers the female body.” The connection brought together two of her enduring interests: “Another great combination for me, feminism and Greece.” Collecting the questions that matter Rather than collecting around a particular movement or medium, Panagopoulos is guided by the questions that occupy her. “I would say that I am collecting subject matters, issues,” she said. “I have questions and problems in my head that I’m looking for answers and solutions to. And I’m looking for those in the works of the artists.” Those questions range from her evolving experience as a woman to the lives of women in neighboring countries. They also extend to conflict and coexistence: “how you resolve issues with other people within your family, within your neighborhood, within your country, with other countries, how you make peace.” “These are all issues that float somewhere in my head, and [are] reflected in the works I collect,” she said. For those beginning to collect, her advice is to look widely and ask questions. “You have to gain criteria,” she said. Her own acquisitions are ultimately guided by “my intuition and how I feel about certain works of art.” She is also wary of the pressures of the market. “There is a lot of noise in the art world, and there’s a lot of pressure, too. Art fairs are like dungeons,” she said. Experience, however, offers a way through. “The more you see art, the more you gain experience, the more you can turn off the noise.” From private collection to public conversation Beyond collecting, Panagopoulos has long supported art institutions, particularly in London. “I chose my favorite institutions,” she said, naming London’s Tate and Delfina Foundation, “which I really love.” Her involvement predates her identity as a collector. “I supported venues and shows, then inevitably I became more involved by joining boards.” The invitation to exhibit at the Hellenic Centre came after its curators visited the collection’s inaugural Athens exhibition. “It was a spontaneous decision,” she said. Although the collection encompasses international artists, Greece remains a central point of reference. Fernweh , a German word expressing a longing for distant places, captures something of this outward-looking perspective. Panagopoulos hopes visitors will leave “feeling a bit more connected to Greece,” and with a deeper curiosity about its relationship to Europe and the wider world. That desire to foster connections also shapes the collection’s permanent space in Athens, which opened in 2025. “We have a lot more visitors than we expected, which is amazing,” she said. “We have museum groups, we have individuals, we have artists, and then we also have the neighborhood that comes.” Alongside the artworks, the space houses an archive and library, encouraging visitors to spend time with the collection on their own terms. “It’s a space that people can come and stay and lounge and take their time to look into the artworks.” Panagopoulos is clear that she does not want to dictate how the works are understood. “I just collect; I don’t curate, and I don’t impose my vision onto others,” she said. “Some people are moved by certain things, some people have their own understanding.” For her, opening the collection to the public has also expanded the meaning of ownership. “So everybody owns part of the collection the way they want to own it.”

title: $12.9 million de Kooning painting leads Sotheby’s October London auctions.
summary: Sotheby's Contemporary Evening Auction in London realized £46 million ($61 million) on October 15th, led by Willem de Kooning 's Untitled (1977), which sold for £9.8 million ($12.9 million) against an estimate of £8 million–£12 million ($10.69 million–$16.03 million)—the highest price ever achieved for a work by the artist at auction in Europe. The sale brought Sotheby’s combined Modern and Contemporary art total in London this year to £598 million ($793 million), the strongest year-to-date figure since 2015 and more than double the equivalent total at this point last year. The evening‘s sale saw strong demand for American abstraction alongside German painting. A monumental Abstraktes Bild (1992) by Gerhard Richter brought £6.7 million ($8.9 million), while a late Untitled (1969) work on paper by Mark Rothko , made during the same period as his celebrated Rothko Chapel paintings, sold for £3.8 million ($5 million). David Hockney ’s Henry Reading fetched £2.8 million ($3.7 million). His iPad drawing 10th–22nd June 2021, Water Lilies in the Pond with Pots of Flowers (2021) sold for nearly three times its high estimate at £1.9 million ($2.5 million), setting a new auction record for any iPad work by the artist. Elsewhere, Andy Warhol ’s Four Marilyns (Reversal Series) (ca. 1979-86) made £2.7 million ($3.6 million), and Georg Baselitz ’s P.D. Idol (1964) and Die Geißelung (1983) sold for £2.4 million ($3.2 million) and £2.2 million ($2.9 million), respectively. Albert Oehlen 's Schwindel (1996) made £1.7 million ($2.2 million). “This evening's results, which bring our running total for the year in London to over $1 billion, are a testament of our belief in the city all year round,” said Alex Branczik, Sotheby's chairman of modern and contemporary art, Europe and Asia. “Our commitment to the London market extends far beyond a single week: we continue to champion the city as a cornerstone of the global art market throughout the year.” Beyond De Kooning, the evening also set a new benchmark for British artist Michael Andrews , whose work sold for £704,000 ($940,000). Sotheby’s reported 7,850 visitors to its Frieze Week exhibition over seven days, and said London’s year-to-date auction total across all categories has now passed $1 billion, its highest since 2018. Sotheby’s London sales continue this today with both a Contemporary Day auction and a dedicated David Hockney sale.

title: The 10 Best Booths at Frieze London and Frieze Masters 2026.
summary: Crisp autumn foliage and the sight of white tents peeking above the trees in Regent’s Park—it could only mean the return of Frieze London and Frieze Masters . The two fairs kicked off their VIP previews on October 14th, drawing a typically well-dressed and spirited crowd, with Helena Bonham Carter, Andrew Garfield, and Tilda Swinton among the famous faces in attendance. It was a colorful, exciting, and—dare we say—jubilant opening, a celebration of the continuing dynamism of London’s art scene, which continues to prove its doubters wrong. Keep calm and carry on? At Frieze, it’s stay suave and shimmy through. With more than 300 booths between them (172 at Frieze London and 140 at Frieze Masters), the fairs are showcasing everything from Triceratops skulls to transgressive sculpture. Frieze London, which is dedicated to contemporary art, has regained a sense of vitality in recent years, perhaps spurred by the arrival of competitor Art Basel Paris across the Channel four years ago (this year’s edition opens next week). Works by established artists are still commonplace here, but many galleries use the opportunity to introduce emerging names and experimental practices to a receptive crowd. Nowhere is this more apparent than in the fair’s Focus section, dedicated to younger galleries, where risk-taking is the order of the day. Visitors might not love everything they see, but the fair is betting they’ll leave with a few discoveries. This year, intriguing art can be found in just about every corner of Frieze, including the restrooms (courtesy of London artist Gray Wielebinski , who has transformed urinal cakes and toilet-rim blocks into scented sculptures). And while Frieze Masters, dedicated to historical art, has a reputation for being more subdued than its contemporary sibling, it too offered plenty of surprises, from lesser-known chapters of established artists’ careers to the Spotlight section, where solo presentations champion pioneering and overlooked figures. The fair also retains its charming eclecticism, with armor, jewelry, and rare books rubbing shoulders with paintings and sculptures by some of art history’s storied names. While both fairs comfortably passed the ambiance check, they are ultimately judged on the strength of their buying activity, which appeared tentatively strong during the opening hours. Sold-out booths on VIP day included Gagosian , Fortes D’Aloia & Gabriel , Alice Amati , and a.SQUIRE, and reported sales were led by Jan Brueghel the Elder ’s Still Life of Flowers in a Stoneware Vase (1607–08) for a price “in the region” of £5 million ($6.57 million) at Hauser & Wirth ’s Frieze Masters stand. “I’ve been in London for every single Frieze Week since the fair’s inception, and I am here to say this city is as busy, energized, exciting, and excited as I ever have seen it,” enthused the gallery’s president Iwan Wirth. “The fair felt much more manageable this year, with a positive energy throughout,” Federica Bonacasa, art advisor at Citi Wealth, told Artsy. “Many of the most in-demand works had been placed early on, and galleries seemed to feel a degree of buoyancy.” The strong presence of international visitors also served as a reminder of London’s enduring status as a global art capital. This week, the city is buzzing with major museum exhibitions, an expanding constellation of satellite fairs , and standout gallery shows , offering plenty for art lovers of all stripes.“It really felt as though people had traveled to London as a destination,” added Bonacasa. Here, we present our 10 best booths from Frieze London and Frieze Masters 2026. White Cube Frieze London, booth D21 With works by Ilana Savdie, John Banting, Hans Bellmer, Louise Bourgeois, Frank Bowling, Alexander Calder, Salvador Dalí, Willem de Kooning, Marlene Dumas, Leonor Fini, Nancy Grossman, Richard Hunt, Gustav Klimt, Maria Lassnig, Jackson Pollock, Egon Schiele, and Yves Tanguy Painter Ilana Savdie , who grew up in Barranquilla, Colombia, returns to her home city’s carnival annually. Last year, one motif kept catching her eye: the alligator. It comes from the myth of the hombre caimán , or “alligator man,” who drinks a potion to spy on women bathing and gets stuck halfway between man and alligator. The motif made its way into the paintings at the heart of White Cube’s booth : huge canvases that undulate with fluorescent forms. “The idea of a hybrid being is a huge part of the work,” the artist said. The alligator is most visible in Lip Lickers (2026), where reptilian mouths gape open. Savdie said the title evokes “someone salivating over a joke,” alluding to the Florida immigration detention center that was nicknamed “Alligator Alcatraz” by the far right. Savdie worked on the paintings side by side over several months, layering them and setting them aside to dry. “I’m dealing with the quick-drying mark and the slow-drying mark, and the friction between the two,” she added. Alongside the new paintings are recent, more minimal ink works with simple, swooping lines, and several 2024 works on paper, including oil monotypes and pen-and-acrylic drawings. This central display, all on standard white booth walls, is surrounded by a sturdy metal grid hung with incredible pieces by major 20th-century names: Egon Schiele , Marlene Dumas , Leonor Fini , Frank Bowling , all artists whose practices have inspired Savdie. Visual echoes emerge between these smaller historical works and Savdie’s paintings. The grasping hands in Salvador Dalí ’s Scène hystérique d’une femme avec tiroir (ca. 1937), for instance, find a counterpoint also visible in Savdie’s The Harbingers (2026). Savdie called these links “incidental.” “It’s coming from such an instinctive place at this point,” she said. The booth was packed on VIP day, making Savdie hard to pin down for an interview. The gallery declined to give prices for the historical works, but Savdie’s range from $15,000 to $325,000. —Josie Thaddeus-Johns Goodman Gallery Frieze London, booth AA6 With works by Unathi Mkonto In his simple curved wooden forms, Unathi Mkonto is exploring new languages for African architecture, drawing inspiration from the land. Mkonto is part of Working Title, Goodman Gallery ’s incubator for emerging African artists, and was nominated by Yinka Shonibare for the gallery’s booth in Frieze’s Artist-to-Artist section. (The pair met in person for the first time at the fair.) Here, the South African artist shows beechwood sculptures inspired by the umbrella tree, whose almost horizontal shape is common across African landscapes, bearing fruits and seeds. At the center of the booth is the largest work, Branching Umbrella (2026), a stacked pile of book-sized panels, from which arm-like extensions stretch more than 15 feet across. Small wooden spheres nestle between these branching rods, forming a minimalist gesture evoking a tree, its branches, and its seeds. For Mkonto, nature remains the best model for how to live. “All these shiny internet things are going to go away,” Mkonto said, “and we’re going to go back to that.” Originally trained in architecture, Mkonto later taught himself woodworking. “I cut the wood into strips and bend it as far as it can go, and then I let it sit for a while, and it takes the shape,” he said. It took him years to understand the material, and he’s still learning. “Every day is something new,” he said. “I don’t get bored of it.” The resulting sculptures are deceptively simple, at once future-oriented and timeless. By the end of the fair’s VIP day, the booth had sold out, with works priced between £8,000 and £15,000 ($10,605 and $19,885). —J.T.-J. Public Gallery Frieze London, booth F25 With works by Steph Huang If your stomach is rumbling after hours of marching around the fair, Steph Huang ’s cheeky booth with Public Gallery will have you salivating. Titled “Lili Deli,” after her 2025 exhibition at Taipei Fine Arts Museum, her solo presentation of hand-blown glass and cast metal works in this year’s excellent Focus section offers “a critical audit of our consumer habits,” said Nicole Estilo Kaiser, the gallery’s director. Among the works are wall sconces made of tins of Perello olives and Lyle’s Golden Syrup, oversized shiny green glass olives, and a bar cart holding a bowl of pink high-fructose syrup (the syrup is real, and the gallery will have to keep flies away from it all week). Born in Taiwan in 1990, Huang now works out of a studio at Studio Voltaire in London. Her practice revolves around two questions, Estilo Kaiser said: “What are we eating, and how is it getting to us?” Each work traces a link in the global supply chain. For instance, Golden Egg’s Matinee (2026) consists of a beautifully hand-hammered copper egg perched on bronze chicken feet inside a circular glass-and-powder-coated steel structure. Almost a furniture piece, it calls attention to industrial farms that “prioritize high yields and rapid growth over the basic welfare of animals,” Estilo Kaiser said. Elsewhere, tiny glass prawns point to shrimp farms in Indonesia, where forests have been cut down to make way for man-made ponds. Other works explore the ingredients hidden in our food. Hold one of the glass slices of bread in Toasted (2026) up to the light and invisible ink reveals “E471,” an emulsifier found in most supermarket bread. Huang doesn’t exempt herself from this scrutiny. Much of what’s on view, including the glass olives, reflects what she eats and recycles. “We are, as consumers, seduced into buying the things that we do,” Estilo Kaiser said. Prices for works range from £7,000 ($9,200) to £12,000 ($15,800). —J.T.-J. Nature Morte Frieze London, booth A12 With works by Aiza Ahmed, Tanya Goel, Subodh Gupta, Jitish Kallat, Bharti Kher, Pushpamala N., Ayesha Singh, and Kuldeep Singh Every figure in Aiza Ahmed ’s installation at Nature Morte has an exaggerated nose. The distinctive feature recurs across the Pakistan-born artist’s unframed paintings on paper and fabric that hang haphazardly from the wall. Repeating the motif of a South Asian man in military dress, Ahmed considers the social pressures to conform to colonial masculinity. “Just because you have a uniform or a costume doesn’t mean the nation can homogenize,” she said. Ahmed is one of three artists making their Frieze London debuts in “The Restless Present.” The booth is curated by Habda Rashid, senior curator of modern and contemporary art at Cambridge’s Fitzwilliam Museum. Rashid brought together artists from India and the South Asian diaspora whose work broadens our understanding of “visual culture, vernacular forms, systems of knowledge beyond the Western canon.” The title, she said, poses a question: “Is our present really static?” This theme is perhaps most explicit in the large inkjet print by photographer Pushpamala N. , who restages Vasco da Gama’s arrival in India as depicted in a 19th-century painting, casting herself in the role of the Portuguese explorer. The editioned work, which is also held in Tate’s collection, is surrounded by an ornate golden frame that emphasizes the theatrical construction of this historical moment, now reimagined through a postcolonial perspective. Another thread running through the booth is the urgency and speed of India’s 20th-century modernization. Reflecting the shift from traditional village life to fast-paced urban centers, Subodh Gupta paints the pots and pans of village cooking “almost into abstraction,” Rashid said. Against raw canvas, this silver cookware is engulfed in blurred, gestural brushstrokes, evoking what has been lost and what remains. —J.T.J. Casa Triângulo and Foundry Seoul Frieze London, booth D6 With works by Fernanda Galvão An alien landscape flourishes across the walls of Casa Triângulo and Foundry Seoul’s shared booth . In her richly colored paintings, Fernanda Galvão conjures fantastical scenes that could depict the bottom of the sea or a desert. In her early twenties, the Brazilian artist, born in 1994, survived cancer twice, said Rodrigo Editore, partner at Casa Triângulo. The experience led her to study her own cells and explore the relationship between the microscopic and the cosmic. “Everything exists in a single cell and also in the whole universe,” he said. Working with charcoal, dry pastel, oil stick, and oil on linen, Galvão builds up hybrid forms that resemble sea anemones or strange plant life, rendered in a bruised palette of browns and blues, shot through with neon. These are “fictional landscapes,” Editore said, where “fictional human beings and nature…exist in different dimensions.” Titles like Acid Pearls , Night Ghosts , and Velvet-flower, Seed-eyes and the Black-hole-shells (all 2026) hint at the otherworldly environments she’s evoking. Her surroundings also seeps into the work. After a trip to Joshua Tree, she started including more dry, desert-like forms in her paintings, as seen in an untitled triptych on view in the booth. Now based in France, Galvão is gaining international momentum. Last summer, she showed alongside David Hockney and Georgia O’Keeffe in “ Alien Shores ,” a group show of strange landscapes at White Cube Bermondsey. She is also one of four winners of the ArtReview x Casa Wabi prize and has recently joined the roster of Berlin gallery Barbara Thumm, where she will have a solo show in July 2027. More than half of the booth’s works had sold by the end of VIP day priced €7,500 to €30,500 ($7,838 to $34,185). —J.T.-J. Takato Kano Gallery Frieze Masters, booth S30 With works by Shiko Munakata Bold black lines, softly bleeding colors, and expressive figures define Takato Kano Gallery ’s striking solo presentation of works by Japanese printmaker Shiko Munakata . Spanning works from the 1950s through the early ’70s, the booth offers a fascinating look at the artist’s experimentation with woodblock printing, a medium he helped push in radical new directions. Munakata drew his subjects from a wide variety of sources, from religious figures to boats, blending spiritual symbolism with everyday subjects. Among the highlights is a series of 10 hanging scrolls each depicting a Buddhist disciple, which relate to works exhibited at the São Paulo Bienal in 1955 and the Venice Biennale in 1956, where Munakata gained international recognition. As gallerist Kano explained, Munakata departed from traditional woodblock techniques by developing urazaishiki , or reverse coloring, applying pigment to the back of thin washi paper rather than its surface. “The black line is the most important, so color never dominates,” Kano said. The resulting soft, diffused hues allow the forceful outlines to remain at the forefront. This interplay of forceful linework and delicate color lends the works an extraordinary vitality. Prices for works range from £9,000 ($11,871) to £650,000 ($857,398). —Arun Kakar David Zwirner and Victoria Miro Frieze Masters, booth D9 With works by Alice Neel As visitors approach David Zwirner and Victoria Miro ’s joint booth, they are greeted by Alice Neel ’s striking 1966 portrait of Beat poet Allen Ginsberg. With his mouth agape and eyes wide behind dark-rimmed glasses, Ginsberg appears mid-exclamation against a swirling backdrop of blues, grays, and whites. The arresting painting offers a fitting introduction to a presentation dedicated to Neel’s portraits of queer individuals and their wider circle. The presentation draws on “At Home: Alice Neel in the Queer World,” an exhibition curated by Hilton Als that debuted at Zwirner Los Angeles in 2024 before traveling to Miro in London last year. Other highlights include Kris Kirsten (1971), whose subject meets the viewer with a direct, defiant gaze, and John Cheim (1979), a portrait of the New York art dealer. The works showcase Neel’s fascination with the people who shaped her world, each portrayed in all their individuality. Few artists captured the complexities of human character through portraits quite like Neel. With her loose, expressive brushwork and unflinching psychological insight, the American painter turned portraiture into an intimate record of the communities around her, often depicting individuals overlooked by the mainstream. The booth is part of the fair’s new “Queering Modernism” initiative, which explores the influence of gender and sexuality on 20th-century art. To this end, the presentation also includes archival materials that shed light on the lives of Neel’s sitters. —A.K. Vigo Gallery Frieze Masters, booth C14 With works by Ibrahim El-Salahi It’s not often that visitors get to see an entirely new side of an artist as celebrated as Ibrahim El-Salahi . Yet Vigo Gallery has brought together a remarkable selection of rarely seen early paintings by the Sudanese modernist , offering a glimpse into a pivotal chapter of his career. Dating from his student years at London’s Slade School of Fine Art between 1955 and 1957, the works show the artist’s experimentation, where he began to dismantle traditional forms of representation in pursuit of his own distinctive visual language. Titled “Pre-Pixel,” the presentation brings together works from the artist’s family collection, most of which have never been publicly exhibited. “He starts breaking down the pictorial plane,” Vigo Gallery’s Sebastian Salisbury told Artsy, describing a crucial turning point in the artist’s development. The fragmented forms and geometric structures of his Untitled paintings from 1956 and 1957, for instance, demonstrate his growing interest in breaking images into smaller, interconnected parts. Their gridlike compositions give the impression of pixels, evoking the visual language of digital imagery decades before its emergence. Often described as a pioneer of African modernism, El-Salahi became the first artist from the continent to receive a retrospective at Tate Modern in 2013. His celebrated practice would go on to fuse Arabic calligraphy, African visual traditions, and Western modernism. Here, visitors encounter the beginnings of that artistic language. Works are priced from £145,000 ($191,265) to £400,000 ($527,630). —A.K. MARUANI MERCIER GALLERY Frieze Masters, booth F5 With works by George Rickey, Josef Albers, Georg Baselitz, Ross Bleckner, Sam Francis, Peter Halley, Alex Katz, Robert Mangold, Allan McCollum, Louise Nevelson, Hermann Nitsch, Georg Karl Pfahler, Ed Ruscha, Pierre Soulages and Andy Warhol. There’s a mesmerizing sense of movement at MARUANI MERCIER ’s booth , where George Rickey ’s delicate kinetic sculptures hang overhead and punctuate the space, their slender metal elements gently shifting with the surroundings (and forcing a few visitors to get out of their way). More than 20 works spanning five decades of the American sculptor’s career take center stage in this elegant presentation, which makes a compelling case for an artist whose influence has arguably outpaced his recognition among collectors. “He is really well known in the art world, in art history,” gallery founder Serge Maruani told Artsy, noting that Rickey’s work is held in more than 180 museums worldwide, yet remains comparatively unfamiliar to collectors. The gallery began representing the artist’s foundation in Europe earlier this year, and the booth includes rarely exhibited works alongside pieces previously shown in museums. Prices for works by the artist range from £14,000 ($18,467) to £200,000 ($263,815). The sculptures are shown alongside two early paintings from Josef Albers ’s iconic “Homage to the Square” series. Rickey considered Albers a mentor, and their works offer contrasting yet complementary explorations of perception, through movement and color respectively. Elsewhere, the booth brings together an impressive roll call of works by post-war heavyweights, including Georg Baselitz , Pierre Soulages , Alex Katz , Ed Ruscha , and Andy Warhol . It’s an emblematic Frieze Masters presentation: museum-caliber names, thoughtfully orchestrated dialogues, and an abundance of visual riches, all assembled with a touch of class. —A.K. Bowman Sculpture Frieze Masters, booth C19 With works by Ossip Zadkine, Eduardo Paolozzi, William Turnbull, Paul Mount, Margaret Lovell, Auguste Rodin, and Helaine Blumenfield. At Bowman Sculpture ’s booth , a pair of hulking metal works by Scottish sculptor Eduardo Paolozzi are designed to be climbed on, crawled through, and played with. These unusual 1970s creations (priced at £120,000—$158,289—each), which sit at the intersection of sculpture, architecture, and playground equipment, offer a fascinating glimpse into a chapter of Paolozzi’s career when the artist was rethinking how art could inhabit public spaces. Created during a period when Paolozzi was collaborating with designer Terence Conran, the sculptures were conceived with children in mind, combining bold, architectural forms with an unexpected sense of play. One features intricate handwoven elements and carefully softened edges, while the other adopts a more angular, architectural form. Both have previously been exhibited at Yorkshire Sculpture Park. “This was a completely different way of looking at sculpture,” gallery director Mica Bowman told Artsy, describing the artist’s ambition to create something “beautiful, architectural, but also that people can engage with.” Elsewhere, the works on view explore the more expressive possibilities of sculpture through Ossip Zadkine ’s Tête d’Orphée (Head of Orpheus) (1956), a Cubist -inspired interpretation of the mythological musician, alongside exemplary works by Auguste Rodin , William Turnbull , and Margaret Lovell. Together, the booth offers a compelling journey through the evolution of modern sculpture, from expressive treatments of the human form to fractured planes and playful architectural experiments. It’s a thoughtfully assembled presentation that invites visitors to consider sculpture as something to experience. —A.K.

title: $41.7 million Kandinsky painting leads Christie’s October London auctions.
summary: In total, Christie’s two evening sales achieved a sell-through rate of 91% by lot and 96% by value. The results marked a 103% increase from the equivalent sales last year, continuing the momentum of the auction house’s London sales in March. “This has been an extraordinary year for London,” said Bonnie Brennan, CEO of Christie’s. “Across the market, we have seen some of the strongest sales the city has witnessed in years, demonstrating London’s enduring importance as a global center for art and collecting.” The evening also included “Monsoon: The Peter Simon Collection,” which generated £107.51 million ($142.34 million), becoming the highest-value single-owner collection ever sold at Christie’s London. The auction, which will be followed up by a day sale and online auction from the same collection, achieved a sell-through rate of 98% by lot, with 43% of lots exceeding their high estimates. Among the collection’s standout results was Liubov Popova ’s Painterly Architectonic (1918), which sold for £7.64 million ($10.12 million), more than four times its £1.8 million ($2.38 million) low estimate. The painting attracted nearly eight minutes of bidding and set a new auction record for the artist. Across the two evening sales, seven notable auction records were established. These included Bridget Riley ’s Streak 2 (1979), which achieved £5.21 million ($6.9 million), and David Bomberg ’s San Miguel, Toledo, Afternoon (1929), which sold for £3.26 million ($4.32 million). Other records were set for Portia Zvavahera , Barbara Hepworth (for a painting), Igshaan Adams , and Gerhard Richter (for a tapestry). Igshaan Adams ’s The certainty of being a rose (ii) (2026), offered to benefit Artists for Climate Action, achieved £96,000 ($127,104), also a new record for the artist. The fundraising initiative brings together the environmental organizations Gallery Climate Coalition and ClientEarth. Following the Kandinsky, Mondrian, and Bacon works, the most expensive lots across Christie’s two evening sales were: Piet Mondrian’s Composition A, with Double Line and Yellow (1935), which sold for £9.71 million ($12.86 million). Joan Miró ’s Peinture (Les amants - Adam et Eve) (1925), which sold for £8.56 million ($11.33 million).

title: $6.6 million Jan Brueghel the Elder painting leads sales at Frieze London and Masters 2026.
summary: A painting by Flemish master Jan Brueghel the Elder led reported sales during the opening day of Frieze London and Frieze Masters 2026, as both fairs welcomed VIPs to Regent’s Park on Wednesday, October 14th. Early transactions shared by galleries pointed to demand across historical and contemporary art, with several reporting sold-out presentations. The top reported sale came from Hauser & Wirth , which placed Brueghel’s Still Life of Flowers in a Stoneware Vase (ca. 1607–08) for around £5 million ($6.64 million) at Frieze Masters. The painting has a remarkable provenance, having previously belonged to the Rothschild collection before being seized by the Nazis and subsequently restituted. “We’ve been selling historical masters alongside contemporary art since the inception of the gallery, but this is an undisputed milestone,” said gallery president Iwan Wirth. “It’s one of the most important works we’ve ever been involved with.” The sale surpassed the leading transaction from last year’s opening day, when Hauser & Wirth sold a painting by Gabriele Münter for $3.01 million. At Frieze London, meanwhile, galleries reported brisk activity across price points, with Alice Amati , Goodman Gallery , Fortes D’Aloia & Gabriel , a.SQUIRE, and Gagosian among those reporting sold-out booths. “London is always an exciting place to be during Frieze Week, and this year is no exception,” art advisor Courtney Pettit told Artsy. “The quality of the institutional presentations is exceptional, complemented by museum-worthy exhibitions across the city’s galleries. The main fair got off to a lively start, with bustling aisles and collectors showing strong engagement and enthusiasm.” Here is a selection of leading sales reported during the fairs’ opening day. Check back on Monday for our full sales report once the fair closes. Top sales at Frieze London and Frieze Masters 2026 Hauser & Wirth also sold Francis Picabia ’s Untitled (ca. 1941–43) for €1.1 million ($1.23 million) and Pablo Picasso ’s Violon (Violin) (1943) for €850,000 ($951,000) at Frieze Masters. At Frieze London, the gallery placed Avery Singer ’s Solver (v.3) (2026) for $800,000 and George Condo ’s Figure Composition (2026) for $600,000. David Zwirner reported a string of seven-figure and six-figure transactions, led by a new painting by Michaël Borremans for $1.5 million. Other highlights included works by Dana Schutz for $900,000, Lisa Yuskavage for $450,000, and Portia Zvavahera for $300,000. A new painting by Sasha Gordon sold to a European museum for $400,000. Thaddaeus Ropac sold Antony Gormley ’s Aside (2025) for £500,000 ($664,000) and Martha Jungwirth ’s Untitled (Berggasse 19) (2026) for €560,000 ($627,000).
