title: 8 Roy Lichtenstein Works that Explain Why the Pop Artist Is So Influential
summary: When Roy Lichtenstein ’s paintings of comic-book characters and glamorous women first appeared in New York galleries in the early 1960s, they challenged some of the most basic assumptions about what painting should be. Instead of the era’s popular gestural abstraction associated with artists like Jackson Pollock and Willem de Kooning , Lichtenstein offered crisp outlines, primary colors, speech bubbles, and enlarged dots that mimicked the printing processes of comics and advertisements (known as benday dots). His images looked mechanical, but they were painstakingly made by hand. Lichtenstein was born in New York in 1923 and began drawing and painting as a teenager, later studying at Ohio State University after taking classes with the artist Reginald Marsh at the Art Students League . After serving in the army during World War II, he returned to the U.S. to teach. His early work bore little resemblance to the Pop paintings that would make him famous: his first New York exhibition, in 1951, was rooted in the Abstract Expressionist idiom then dominating the city’s art scene. By the late 1950s, however, Lichtenstein was experimenting with imagery drawn from popular culture. In 1961, he began making the comic- and advertisement-based paintings that established his signature style. The shift marked the beginning of a sustained investigation into how images are made, reproduced, and understood. Today, Lichtenstein is regarded as one of the defining figures of Pop art, known for questioning what happens to an image when it is copied and transformed into something new—raising questions of authorship and perception. These questions are at the center of “Roy Lichtenstein: Like New,” the Whitney Museum of American Art ’s retrospective, the first in New York devoted to the artist since 1993. On view through May 10, 2027, the exhibition features roughly 130 works from the early 1940s through the 1990s, including painting, drawing, sculpture, and film. The exhibition is organized by Meg Onli, curator at the Whitney, as well as artist Alex Da Corte , and finds connections between one of the early masters of reproduction and today’s digital world. Here are eight works that reveal why Lichtenstein’s deceptively simple images remain so influential. Girl with Ball , 1961 A quintessential image of carefree American leisure in which a young woman in a bathing suit holds a beach ball against a bright sky, Girl with Ball is based on an advertisement for the Mount Airy Lodge in Pennsylvania’s Pocono Mountains. The work illustrates Lichtenstein’s early interest in transforming subjects from advertisements into paintings. The act of transformation is crucial. Lichtenstein was not copying an advertisement; he was turning a commercially produced image into a painting while making the mechanics of its reproduction conspicuous. He flattened colors, exaggerated outlines, eliminated details, and began using his signature benday dots. The painting also marks a major turning point in Lichtenstein’s career. In 1961, he moved away from the Abstract Expressionist vocabulary that had shaped his earlier work and toward the commercial imagery that would make him famous. The transition gave him a new way to investigate painting: by making images that appeared impersonal or mass-produced while requiring considerable control and labor to create. Look Mickey , 1961 Look Mickey, 1961 Roy Lichtenstein Philadelphia Museum of Art In addition to reimagining advertisements, Lichtenstein’s early foray into Pop art was defined by his interest in comic imagery. One of his best-known pieces, Look Mickey , features Mickey Mouse and Donald Duck fishing from a dock, with Donald declaring, “Look Mickey, I’ve hooked a big one!!” The joke is that Donald has actually hooked his own jacket. Lichtenstein based the painting on an illustration from the 1960 children’s book Donald Duck: Lost and Found , simplifying the original composition and reducing its colors to a limited palette of primary hues and white. What made the painting startling in 1961 was not simply its subject. Lichtenstein treated cartoon imagery with the scale, seriousness, and materiality traditionally associated with fine-art painting. The characters were instantly familiar, but the context was entirely different. Leo Castelli Gallery Handshake Poster , 1962 Hanging outside a freestanding gallery built within the museum is a poster from Lichtenstein’s first ever exhibition with Leo Castelli, the influential dealer who helped launch the careers of some of the most famous names in American Pop and Minimalist art. Featuring a handshake, the poster marks one of the most significant moments in the artist’s career. The show, which took place in early 1962, helped to establish the commercial legitimacy of his works despite their unconventional subjects and style. In a standout moment in the show, the museum has recreated this pivotal exhibition, complete with a parquet floor. Bringing the pieces from this show together again, the room in “Like New” offers viewers the chance to step back in time and imagine what it was like to see Lichtenstein’s works when they were first presented. Included in the display are images based on war comics, household products like a washing machine, and advertisements, subjects the artist would quickly become known for. Likewise, the historic hanging offers insight into Lichtenstein’s early adoption of the visual language he would soon master. Drowning Girl , 1963 Lichtenstein’s Drowning Girl has become widely recognizable as one of the artist’s most famous works. The piece features a woman floating in turbulent water, her eyes closed and her face set in an expression of melodramatic distress. A thought bubble reads, “I don’t care!” Lichtenstein based the work on an image by comic-book illustrator Tony Abruzzo that appeared in DC Comics ’ Secret Hearts in 1962, cropping the original composition and removing the woman’s boyfriend to concentrate attention on her isolated figure. That process of cropping and editing is central to understanding the painting. Lichtenstein took an already manufactured image and manufactured it again. By enlarging the comic-book panel and transferring its visual language onto canvas, he transformed something designed for mass circulation into something that would hang in a museum. By this point, Lichtenstein was one of the most visible young artists associated with Pop art. It was clear Pop art was growing, but it was seen as radical, even offensive. Lichtenstein and other Pop artists pushed forward despite negative criticism, continuing to depict popular culture and the consumerist tendencies of American life at a time when the U.S. was beginning to define itself as in opposition to Communism. Hot Dog , 1964 In Hot Dog , Lichtenstein took an ordinary object of American life and transformed it into an unmistakably Pop image. He would come to depict an image of a hot dog often, including in color form, while the one on view in “Like New” is a black-and-white work on paper. Lichtenstein’s interest in everyday objects was part of a larger Pop-art challenge to the idea that serious art should deal with elevated subjects. By giving the hot dog the scale and visual authority of a traditional, museum-worthy painting, Lichtenstein challenged the distinction between “high” and “low” culture. The subject has acquired another layer of significance at the Whitney. Artist and exhibition co-curator Alex Da Corte has installed Hot Dog with Ketchup (2026), a billboard across from the museum, based on Lichtenstein’s painting. The intervention turns Lichtenstein’s Pop image back into something public-facing and commercial-looking, while also referencing the actual NYC food vendors outside the museum. Little Big Painting , 1965 With Little Big Painting , Lichtenstein turned his attention from comic-book imagery to painting itself. The work depicts large, carefully rendered brushstrokes in red, yellow, white, and black, a motif he revisited often in his practice. The target of the brushstroke pieces was the heroic gestural language of Abstract Expressionism, the dominant American art movement of the preceding generation. Artists like Pollock had made the physical act of painting central to their work, with drips, splashes, and sweeping marks serving as evidence of the artist’s individual presence. Lichtenstein took that supposedly spontaneous gesture and turned it into a reproducible graphic symbol. Behind the large strokes in the work is a field of benday dots, associating the supposedly unique, expressive brushstroke with mass production. Rouen Cathedral, Set III , 1968–69 Lichtenstein’s Rouen Cathedral, Set III reimagines one of the canonical achievements of 19th-century painting: Claude Monet ’s series of paintings of Rouen Cathedral. Monet famously painted the cathedral repeatedly under changing conditions of light, producing some 30 versions in the 1890s. Lichtenstein turned their serial structure into his own Pop-art experiment. While Monet used subtle shifts of color and brushwork to capture fleeting changes in atmosphere, Lichtenstein translated the cathedral into stark contrasts and enlarged benday dots across five canvases. This is one of the clearest instances of Lichtenstein borrowing from other artists—seen in several artworks on view at the Whitney that reference recognizable pieces from artists like Henri Matisse and Pablo Picasso . Comparing each of the five canvases, the Rouen Cathedral set also offers a remarkable case study in how Lichtenstein used dots and color. At close range, the dots look like discrete painted circles; from farther away, they merge into tones and colors, particularly noticeable on the canvases with dark-blue and light-yellow backgrounds. In this respect, Lichtenstein’s paintings form an interesting counterpoint to Monet’s. Both depend on the viewer’s perception to capture the same object, but using radically different means. Mirror #1 (Oval 60” x 48”) , 1969 In Lichtenstein’s famous “Mirror” series (1969–72), he portrayed a familiar object—a reflective surface—as something that isn’t reflective at all. The exhibition contains eight of these iconic works. In each, the mirror is represented through a circular or oval composition of colored bands and halftone dots. Seen well in Mirror #1 , instead of giving viewers a literal reflection, Lichtenstein offers the graphic signs that tell us what a mirror is supposed to look like. Rendered in black-and-white dots, the composition contains depictions of a glare, as if reflecting light. Removing the mirror’s function, the object becomes an image of itself. The work also complicates the assumption that Lichtenstein’s art was simply about copying mass media. Mirrors became another way for him to explore perception and illusion. His treatment of the reflective surface makes this simple object conspicuously artificial. Here, the viewer can see Lichtenstein not simply as the artist who turned comics into paintings, but as an artist preoccupied with what happens when images move from one context into another. These mirror works promise to show us reality while giving us only another constructed surface. And that may be the key to seeing Lichtenstein “Like New,” as the exhibition title frames the works. His paintings are instantly recognizable because they look like things we have seen before. But the longer we look, the more complicated that recognition becomes.

title: Remembering Artist Sarah Cunningham through the Eyes of Those Who Knew Her
summary: Sarah Cunningham was a rising star in the art world whose trajectory was brought to a tragic halt when she died at the age of 31 in 2024. Part of The Artsy Vanguard 2023–24 , the Nottingham-born artist was widely admired for her fantastical wildernesses and forestscapes that she brought vividly to life via sweeping expressionistic brushstrokes that thrum with the force of nature. Now, the artist has a major retrospective, “ Sarah Cunningham: Midnight Sun ,” on show at Nottingham Contemporary through January 10th, 2027, the hometown institution where she actually worked as a gallery assistant in 2019. Here, the show’s co-curator Katie Simpson, who knew Cunningham personally, shares her memories of the artist with Artsy, alongside other colleagues and collaborators who knew and worked with her. Katie Simpson, curator, Nottingham Contemporary Sarah was a force, incredibly strong headed, articulate, kind, spiritual, and compassionate, someone who truly saw beauty in the world and wanted to learn everything she could about different people, communities, histories, nature, and coexistence of all living entities. She was a serious and dedicated artist, curious and generous in conversations about her work, incredibly supportive and caring towards others and was loved and respected dearly. Her work is powerfully visceral and dynamic, from large works to the smallest ones, each hold a special power and spiritual quality. Her confidence in markmaking and color mixing, her ability to create new worlds that pull you into the canvas is rare and extremely compelling. Co-curator Niall Ó Faircheallaigh and I were immediately drawn to three works: The World It Softly Lulls (2021), Via Lucis (2023), and Starshine and Clay (2022) which we felt encapsulated the main considerations and themes for Sarah and her work. We were drawn to her use of tone and color, and her interest in the blending of time: day and night, dawn and dusk, and elements of sci-fi and world building. The title draws you in like the works themselves—what does a world with a midnight sun look like? It speaks to the immersive aspect of Sarah’s work, she was not just thinking representationally in order to depict landscapes or recognizable forms, but materially, spiritually, and immersively, to help us see beyond the limits of our worlds and imagine new possibilities. It feels incredibly special that we’re able to host so much of her work in our galleries in this homecoming show. We hope the exhibition brings new audiences to her work as well as giving those who knew and loved her a space to celebrate her and spend time with so many of her incredible paintings in one place. Louise Hayward, partner, Lisson Gallery , London I first saw Sarah’s work at her exceptional degree show at the Royal College of Art (RCA), London. There was the most compelling abstract, yet somehow figurative landscape painting, only 30cm by 20cm. It was perfection and I couldn’t believe such a young artist had found their path from feeling to form in such a profound way. Sarah effervesced with creativity; everything about her from the way she spoke about her experiences in the rainforest in Panama to life as a courier driving alone at night, to the delight she felt as turpentine changed the nature of her brushstrokes. She delighted in the world around her, from the great to the smallest of details, finding something to consider with sincerity and passion that may find a way into a composition. I loved hanging out with Sarah in her studio—it was an extension of her being. She loved to paint, at night, when the rest of the city was quiet. She kept books with her poetry, her brushes still dipped in paint and every inch of space covered with canvases. When we spoke, she drew me into a world of leaves embedding us shawl-like in her embrace of the world around her. Max Bossier, director, Lisson Gallery, London I first discovered Sarah’s work online in 2021. I contacted her shortly after and we met at her Royal College of Art studio in London for the first time. She had prepared a small showroom display and I was absolutely blown away by the quality of the work. Her painting style was so radical and new. I have never met a young artist who had such a maturity in her work before. The way Sarah composed her paintings out of sheer intuition, the energy in her work, and her incredibly distinct way of bringing colors to life were incomparable. My most beautiful memory of working with Sarah was definitely our trip to Los Angeles in 2024 to open her solo show at Lisson L.A. She had never been to the West Coast before and we explored my favorite places together for a week. Sarah worked on her paintings in the gallery until minutes before the opening, despite us insisting that she leave them—she was a perfectionist! The exhibition was wonderful and ended up being a huge success. Dr. Jesse Ash, senior tutor in painting at the Royal College of Art, London At college, Sarah’s presence was precious—she listened to those around her in a way that gave a deep respect and charge to the words of others and always offered carefully considered, generous input with a calm, warm, honest attentiveness. But what I remember most vividly is the transition in her face from a furrowed brow of serious concentration—maybe listening to someone or making sense of something—and then in a moment, breaking and changing her expression to the most illuminated, warm, and open smile. Jo Dennis , artist Sarah and I would usually meet in a pub, just the two of us, and talk for hours. She would also send me rambling voice notes. We talked a lot about painting and what was going on in our studios, but also about books. We both loved J.G. Ballard and would often end up talking about his novels in relation to what we were making. Sarah was incredibly warm, self-effacing and very funny. But when she talked about her work there was a real intensity to her. She was completely serious about painting without ever being self-important about it. Fran Copeman, artist Sarah exploded into my life after a pint in the pub. It was there we had the first of many great conversations where I was quietly in admiration of how fun and funny she was with a sense of purpose in life without all the boring filters that a lot of people have. We are lucky to have all her wisdom and honesty locked within her paintings and I cannot wait to see them again. Laurence Watchorn , artist An edited extract from a letter written to Sarah after her death and read at her memorial service at the RCA All who knew your pictures felt the command of your brushstrokes and brilliance imbued in them but it was who you were as a human that resonated through and beyond the pigment. We connected over life’s challenges and became friends through our shared passion and drive to synthesize our relationship with nature into our own visual languages. You’d come alive at dusk and toil in the dawn-lit hours to channel deep, creative forces. I remember a deep chat about a particular diptych of yours, Via Lucis , which you worked on tirelessly. You pushed through those extremely difficult moments which all painters will understand and broke through into what is a truly unique and momentous painting. You proved it was possible for people of a certain background to carve a path in the art world and did so by being unapologetically yourself.

title: Digital art gallery and platform TAEX to open new Monaco space.
summary: TAEX , a contemporary art gallery and curated digital art platform founded in London in 2020, has opened its first permanent gallery in Monaco. The gallery, located in the Mareterra, a new waterfront district, is inaugurating the space with “Testing Ground,” a solo exhibition by Paris-based conceptual artist Kevin Abosch , on view through November 30th. The gallery occupies Le Renzo, a landmark building developed by Pritzker Prize–winning architect Renzo Piano . Since its founding, TAEX has built an international program with presences at Art Basel , Paris Photo , ART SG , and Tokyo Gendai , alongside collaborations with major artists including Marina Abramović . The gallery has previously had presentations during the 2025 Monaco Grand Prix and a special integration featuring Abramović at that year's artmonte-carlo fair. “Having supported arts and culture in Monaco for many years, I am especially proud to open TAEX Gallery here,” said the gallery’s founder Inna Bazhenova. “Monaco has long been a place where cultural ambition and international perspectives meet, and our permanent space in Mareterra marks a new chapter in our commitment to the cultural life of the ” For “Testing Ground,” TAEX presents new, previously unseen works from Abosch's latest body of synthetic photography, created specifically for the Monaco space, alongside pieces from his series “Ethical Work,” first shown by TAEX at Paris Photo in 2025, and the rare 2010 work Potato #345 . This exhibition centers on Abosch's synthetic photography, a genre he originated in which computational processes generate images that retain photography's visual language while depicting places that do not exist. For more than three decades, Abosch has explored what makes an image matter, working across photography, installation, moving image, and generative technologies. His work has been presented at the State Hermitage Museum, the National Museum of China, Fotografiska , the Jeu de Paume, and the Irish Museum of Modern Art. “Our ambition is to make TAEX Monaco a vibrant cultural destination, a place for discovery, exchange and creative dialogue,” said Stefanie De Regel, director of TAEX Monaco. “Against the exceptional backdrop of Mareterra, we want to bring together art and culture in their many expressions, fostering new encounters, collaborations and ideas within Monaco's cultural landscape.”

title: Cindy Sherman fronts Chanel's 2026 Arts & Culture magazine.
summary: Cindy Sherman is the cover star of Volume 2 of the Chanel Culture Fund’s Arts & Culture magazine, due out on October 23rd. The photographer also appears in an extended spread of new self-portraits. The free publication, running to roughly 300 pages, will be distributed through 32 independent bookstores and magazine shops, as well as select partner arts institutions, across 17 countries. For her contribution, Sherman was sent rolls of raw, unsewn vintage fabric and costume jewelry drawn from Chanel’s Patrimoine archive, material she then cut and draped herself to construct the costumes for her new cast of characters, as Vanity Fair reported . “I said, ‘Well, is it okay if I cut things up, cut holes into them and whatnot?’” Sherman told the magazine of her approach to the archival textiles. Describing her longtime interest in photographing older women, she added, “Who the fuck wants to look at pictures of old ladies anyway?” A selection of the resulting photographs is currently on view at Hauser & Wirth 's Mayfair gallery through December 23rd, opening coinciding with this year's Frieze Londo n. The issue also carries original, handwritten lyrics by musician and visual artist Patti Smith , composed in tribute to the ten recipients of the 2026 CHANEL Next Prize, the house's biennial award supporting early-career artists across disciplines. Beyond its two cover contributors, Volume 2 includes profiles of artists Linder Sterling and Klára Hosnedlová , essays on Peggy Guggenheim and Jean Cocteau , and conversations with artists including Nairy Baghramian , Adam Pendleton , Rachel Rose , and Alvaro Barrington . Yana Peel, Chanel's president of arts, culture and heritage, has positioned the magazine as a vehicle for the house’s broader cultural philanthropy, pairing major figures in visual art, music, and writing within a single, non-commercial publication. “At the heart of the work of the CHANEL Culture Fund is cultivating care for ideas, for artists, and for the irreplaceable act of making something new. “Our Arts & Culture magazine is where that practice leaves its trace,” said Peel in a statement. “There could be no one better to grace the cover of Vol.2 than Cindy Sherman, who for five decades has examined the construction of identity and the power over personae that women hold.”

title: Painter Robin F. Williams Channels Botticelli into Glossy Takes on Contemporary Technology
summary: Brooklyn-based painter Robin F. Williams has been thinking about how rapid technological advancement collides with religion. Add internet-fueled psychosis into the mix, and the painter believes we’re entering a moment of rapturous, New Age spirituality. This perspective is apparent in Williams’s new canvas I Am Not a Robot (all works 2026), in which a figure with an infinity-sign-shaped halo stares into a smartphone. “She’s tarot, but she’s also a Catholic angel, but she’s also a New Age light being, or an alien,” Williams recently told me in their Brooklyn studio. “Most of all, she’s confused about her role amid tech’s present reign, confounded by the constant digital overload, which I think is creating this sort of weird, ecstatic, loosening of a grip.” I Am Not a Robot, 2026 Robin F. Williams P.P.O.W Spooky Action at a Distance, 2026 Robin F. Williams P.P.O.W I Am Not a Robot is among eight paintings by Williams that are christening New York gallery P.P.O.W’s first-ever international pop-up in London and on view through October 24th. The solo show, titled “ Act Natural ,” encapsulates our absurd, tech-happy times. Williams made this series over the last year and a half, uniting references from art history and current events in planes of superflat paint. Throughout the works, transparent, glossy acrylic fields combine with waves of metallic oils that simulate holograms. Altogether, they convey the Technicolor cacophony of the information age. Robin F. Williams’s early style Williams started working with oil paint in grade school. In 2014, eight years after graduating from the Rhode Island School of Design, they joined Instagram and abandoned the academically charged medium. They began experimenting with more craft-based methods like airbrush and paint marbling, largely picked up from Instagram’s ascendant DIY arts community. Williams, in turn, started posting their own tutorials. “I didn’t want to just extract,” they said. They recently launched a Substack to offer more in-depth instruction, on a less fraught platform. The artist also remains materially driven—“Act Natural” marks their first time painting on oil-primed linen and using Stuart Semple’s vantablack replica. Medium Mermaid, 2026 Robin F. Williams P.P.O.W Since the pandemic, Williams has mostly made paintings inspired by horror films, which they consider a vehicle for collective catharsis. “I think all art does that,” they said. “Some forms do it at broader scales. But I’m interested in tapping into whatever those feelings are, and making places for collective processing around it.” Such works anchored Williams’s latest exhibitions, including “Undying” at Perrotin Tokyo and “Good Mourning” at P.P.O.W., both in 2024. New work for P.P.O.W.’s London pop-up “Act Natural,” on the other hand, is more of a psychological thriller, tinged with elements of science fiction. While Williams suspects the hype and fear surrounding AI has conjured an egregore, an esoteric entity that arises from the collective consciousness, they also remain open-minded about AI. “I am just not interested in the way it’s turning into every other financial instrument, and recreating every other folly, every other bubble,” they said. “I think it has so much more potential to do wonderful things for our consciousness, but we’re choosing to enslave it and repeat history.” Williams’s equal embrace of the academic and vernacular was especially apparent on the mood board they created to inspire the show. Near a window overlooking Manhattan, Williams had affixed dozens of printed photographs of artworks by abstractionist Paul Klee and pioneering realist Éduoard Manet , pages from Sports Illustrated , and outputs from DALL-E, the bygone AI image generator. “When I was painting about horror, I was taking a lot of screenshots and photos of my TV,” Williams said. “This body of work felt like the references were coming from everywhere.” Language Model, 2026 Robin F. Williams P.P.O.W Sleight of Hand, 2026 Robin F. Williams P.P.O.W Williams’s art historical inspirations were similarly invested in moments of transition: “the modernists or the Cubists that weren’t quite Cubists, or the Renaissance painters that were on the cusp,” they said. They cite Botticelli , whose blend of pagan and Catholic deities inspired this show’s working title, “Lesser Gods.” FLAG Art Foundation teased this new chapter in Williams’s practice this past May, when they exhibited Language Model as part of its recurring Spotlight program. The painting, which reappears in “Act Natural,” depicts a voluptuous, Technicolor nude who poses on a beach at sunset. Devoid of specific natural details, the figure reads as an archetype. The title suggests the affinities between AI and dysmorphia-inducing fashion photography, which feels quaint today when compared with “ Instagram face. ” Here, Williams references the “body positivity” many magazines toyed with in the 2010s. “It just reeks of insincerity now, especially when you look at what they thought a plus-size model was,” Williams said. They’re curious if today’s “models” will rebel like the language they’re based on—itself a flawed technology that eschews consensual meanings. Tempering Better Angels, 2026 Robin F. Williams P.P.O.W Holy Thirst Trap, 2026 Robin F. Williams P.P.O.W Williams’s new tech bro paintings While Williams’s female figures appear as mythic chimeras, their male counterparts are ethereal, shortsighted tech bros lifted straight from Botticelli’s Madonna of the Pomegranate (ca. 1487). In Holy Thirst Trap , they contemplate a glass of water, which AI needs to survive. In Tempering Better Angels , they wade recklessly into wet depths. Williams imagines they’re hyping each other up to get rich off the AI boom. Both paintings evoke the phrase “the tip of the iceberg” by depicting, respectively, a straw and two phalluses beneath the water’s surface. “It’s been interesting to watch the millennial arc of tech bros who started in this very idealistic place,” Williams said. Today, those utopists are organizing disaster bunkers in New Zealand: “It’s just a race for them to escape accountability. How quickly that happened.” The overwhelming beauty of the artist’s new work combats pervasive accelerationism by making viewers stop, agog. Contrary to popular belief, there’s still time to slow this AI race, put the egregore back in its box. “Being in a heightened state makes you much more easily influenced,” Williams said. “That’s the other reason I think painting is still so important.”

title: This Ski-Resort-Turned-Sculpture-Park Carries the Spirit of Land Art into a New Era
summary: Pioneering land artist Nancy Holt felt connected to the desert of the American West from her very first visit in 1968. A few years later, she discovered a stretch of “flat desert ringed by low mountains” in northwestern Utah, where she would create her best-known work, Sun Tunnels (1973–76): a quartet of 18-foot-long concrete cylinders positioned to capture the sunrise and sunset during the solstices. “I wanted to bring the vast space of the desert back to human scale,” Holt wrote in 1977. In the 1960s and ’70s, while land artists like Holt, Robert Smithson , and Michael Heizer headed into remote landscapes, away from cities and galleries, another outdoor model was gaining ground. Founded in 1960, Storm King Art Center in New York’s Hudson Valley helped popularize the modern sculpture park. In the decades since, destinations like Naoshima Island in Japan and Inhotim in Brazil have drawn droves of art lovers into nature. Established in 2024, Powder Art Foundation (PAF) has been taking its own novel approach to the sculpture park, installing ambitious outdoor artworks across 8,000 acres of Powder Mountain, a sprawling ski resort in northern Utah. In winter, you can ski past a Jenny Holzer boulder, pause to ring a bronze bell by Davina Semo hanging from the trees, or glide beneath a string of chandeliers by Kayode Ojo . In summer and fall, the same works can be explored for free, along hiking trails that wind through the mountain. Powder Art Foundation’s vision Powder is home to 16 artworks and counting, with new additions added each year and a forthcoming pavilion that will house a work by James Turrell . Led by chief creative officer Alex Zhang, PAF is transforming the ski resort, which is owned by Netflix co-founder Reed Hastings. The pair bonded over their shared love of Naoshima, known for its incredible art and architecture, though Hastings had a more practical pitch for Powder: “How about like Storm King on a mountain?” Zhang sought to find out: “Could you essentially retrofit a ski resort into a sculpture park, but still keep the soul and the character of the resort intact?” He envisioned the art program as a “whole new cultural layer” extending across the mountain. There’s no target number of works, and no set criteria for the type of art or artist—each piece must feel right for the place. Utah’s history of land art and its ancient Indigenous petroglyphs were also important to the vision. Holt’s Sun Tunnels and Smithson’s Spiral Jetty (1970) are both within driving distance of Powder Mountain. And PAF partners with Dia Art Foundation , which owns those two works and collaborates with the Holt-Smithson Foundation to preserve them. Holt is represented at Powder, too: Her Starfire (1986), comprising eight fire pits arranged to mirror the Big Dipper and North Star, has found a permanent home on top of the mountain, facing the sunset. For his part, Hastings said he doesn’t collect art for himself; rather, “the collection is here,” shared on the mountain. Hiking along the Powder art trail One October morning, I joined a guided hike along the art trail, which you can start at the top of the mountain. The first three sculptures we encountered, all new for the 2026 season, sit nestled among tall evergreens and the flickering yellow leaves of aspen trees. The first work is Rose Wylie ’s Pale-Pink Pineapple/Bomb (2025), a glossy, candy-colored painted bronze that stands more than 10 feet tall and resembles the titular fruit, with a cheeky fleshiness. It’s a rare work for Wylie, who is primarily known for her paintings, and marks her first public sculpture in the U.S. Just minutes away sits Holzer’s THE EYE (2026), a 300-million-year-old quartzite boulder engraved with a line by Utah-born poet May Swenson’s work The Promontory Moment (1956): “The eye also a sun wanders and all that it sees it owns.” After a painstaking search for the right rock, Holzer had the text inscribed on-site to preserve the surrounding landscape. The piece reflects humanity’s long history of leaving marks on the land and is the first of a body of work Holzer will create on the mountain. Farther along is Shanghai-based artist Xu Zhen ’s Hello (2021–22), a twisting, snakelike Corinthian column that exemplifies his practice of colliding East and West. The work is perfectly perched on a mound, encircled by an aspen grove, and, like several works, can be seen from above on the ski lift. One of the art trail’s most striking works is Nobuo Sekine ’s Phase of Nothingness – Stone Stack (1970/2025). The Japanese Mono-ha artist, who died in 2019, conceived the work in 1970 but never saw it realized. More than five decades later, his estate helped bring it to life. Rising about 19 feet, the sculpture is a pile of smooth stones gently leaning into the sky, set against a majestic view of the surrounding slopes and trees. Perhaps the most unexpected work is Ojo’s “…and that they hadn’t heard us calling, still do not hear us, up here in the tree house…” (2025), 21 crystal chandeliers suspended among the trees. Bought from Amazon and reinforced to withstand the mountain’s extreme weather, the ordinary fixtures take on an otherworldly presence. Skiing with art Come ski season, the experience transforms. Ojo’s chandeliers sparkle above the snow, and Sekine’s stones rise from a blanket of white. The resort has a team of “terrain specialists,” effectively art handlers on snowboards, who maintain the works through winter. Semo’s three patinated bronze bells, Mother (2020–24), Listener (2020–24), and Reflector (2025), hang from trees near the tops of challenging runs, inviting skiers to ring them before descending. “I was thinking about skiing as an activity that’s both exhilarating and where you’re in your own head,” Semo told me. “This moment of interiority where you’re skiing and being able to have a moment of reflection before you go down a run.” Semo first visited Powder Mountain before much of the art had been installed. “It was kind of mind-boggling to imagine getting to put the work here,” she said. “The landscape is so vast and natural.” It’s similar to the overwhelming scale Holt faced in the desert, and an idea that inspired Zhang early on: “that relationship from the body to the art to the landscape.”

title: Tribeca loft featuring original Keith Haring mural listed for $25 million.
summary: A triplex loft in Tribeca, featuring a 1979 Keith Haring mural painted directly onto the structure, has come to market for $25 million. The 8,000-square-foot unit, located at 260 West Broadway in the landmarked American Thread Building, is listed with Compass real estate. Haring made the work while a student at the School of Visual Arts (SVA). The school kept a student gallery space on the lower floor of the building at the time—now the first level of the triplex. He made the energetic monochrome mural with a mix of shoe polish and alcohol, atypical materials that make the artwork’s survival over the past 50 years ever more remarkable. Haring painted directly onto an iron column, a structural beam, and the ceiling, meaning it cannot be removed or relocated. The black-and-white mural features interlocking forms typical of the street artist’s iconic line work. When SVA vacated the space in the early 1980s and it became a restaurant, the mural was covered over with wallboard, inadvertently protecting it for decades. It remained hidden until the building's previous owners uncovered it in 2007 and found it largely intact. The current owner, Adam Zoia, chief executive of Glocap Tech, recognized the work immediately when he encountered it. “It was so obviously a Keith Haring. His style is so distinct,” he told the New York Times , noting that the unsigned piece has since been authenticated by the Keith Haring Foundation. Zoia purchased the loft in 2021 and undertook a two-year, floor-to-ceiling renovation around the mural, ultimately building a bar in front of it as a physical buffer to prevent visitors from touching or splashing it. “What kind of a bar in New York City has an original Keith Haring painting on the wall behind it, and painted on the ceiling of the bar, too?” he said. For Zoia, parting with the artwork is harder than parting with the apartment itself. “This kid made something spectacular,“ he said of Haring, who was in his early 20s and years from international fame when he painted it. He estimated that the mural alone, if it could somehow be extracted, would likely be worth more than the loft surrounding it. Art dealer Jenn Singer, founder of a namesake Manhattan gallery, called the mural’s integration into the architecture central to its significance and to the challenge of pricing it. “The site-specific dimension is the real complexity,” she explained to the Times . “Works made for a particular space and physically integrated into it exist in a different market category altogether.” The new owner will effectively become a steward for the work. “Each owner of this loft is its caretaker for their time with it. Every future owner of this space becomes its guardian,” added Singer.

title: All the Art You Need to See During Frieze London 2026
summary: Nothing feels quite like fall in the art world more than venturing into the bright white tents of Frieze London and Frieze Masters nestled among the changing foliage of Regent’s Park. Every October, the art fairs bring with them a citywide feast of exhibitions, satellite fairs, and happenings around town. It may be the best time to experience London’s robust gallery scene—from big names in Mayfair to rising talents at the city’s younger galleries—not to mention its world-class museums. And this year promises not to disappoint. Here’s our 10-stop guide to making the most of Frieze Week 2026. All of the stops below are also featured in City Guide, a new feature in the Artsy app that helps you discover art nearby, save the shows, galleries, and fairs you want to see, and build your own art itineraries. Check it out here . 1. Frieze London, Frieze Masters, and Frieze Sculpture Oct. 14–18 | Regent’s Park Let’s start with the main event. This year, Frieze London and Frieze Masters bring together almost 300 galleries from 48 countries across two tents in Regent’s Park. Frieze London is focused squarely on contemporary art, while Frieze Masters spans thousands of years of art history—from antiquities through the 20th century. Both fairs open with their VIP days on the 14th, with public admission from the afternoon of October 15. At Frieze London, I tend to head first to Focus, the section devoted to younger galleries and emerging artists—and reliably one of the best places to make a discovery. Another favorite is Artist-to-Artist, which invites established artists to select emerging voices for solo presentations. New this year, The Code Universe section looks at art through the lens of popular culture, from the late 1970s to today. Frieze Masters is across the park, but on the way there—it can be a good 20-minute walk—stop by Frieze Sculpture , the fair’s public art program. This year’s edition features works by 11 artists, including Angel Otero , Conrad Shawcross , and Ivana Bašić . Frieze Masters tends to feel a little calmer in atmosphere, with historical works, rediscoveries, unexpected pairings of old and new, and plenty of gems from both familiar and lesser-known names. This year, six presentations take their cues from two remarkable homes: Luis Barragán ’s Casa Barragán in Mexico City and Charles and Maggie Jencks’s Cosmic House in Holland Park. 2. Minor Attractions and Fitzrovia galleries Oct. 13–17 | The Newman, 50 Newman St. | Fitzrovia this heat is making my pores leak, 2023 Madeline Brice Blah Blah Gallery A short walk from Regent’s Park, you’ll find Minor Attractions and a strong cluster of galleries across Fitzrovia and Soho. Now in its fourth edition, the alternative fair—traditionally staged in hotel rooms—has a new home at The Newman in Fitzrovia. More than 75 galleries and nonprofit spaces are taking part this year, filling the hotel with art alongside programming that spans music, performance, and nightlife. Entry is free, and the whole thing promises a freewheeling alternative to the main fairs. While you’re in the area, make time for a few nearby gallery shows too: Timur Si-Qin at Albion Jeune : Si-Qin drew inspiration from the Peruvian Amazon, turning tree trunks, roots, leaves, and other vegetation into stainless steel sculptures that draw attention to the wilderness that still exists. Sophie Birch at Alice Amati : For her first London solo show, Birch presents new paintings shaped by memory, atmosphere, and a recent residency in Rome. Books, houses, bodies, and mosaic floors recur throughout. “ Backstage machinations ” at Night Café : This two-artist show of Isabella Amram and Juliet Dodson brings together painting and sculpture around the figure of the trickster, exploring concealment, illusion, and the ways our perception can be manipulated. 3. Mayfair galleries, London Invitational, and PAD London Various locations | Mayfair You could easily devote several days to Mayfair—London’s densest gallery district—alone this week. Start with the fairs: PAD London (October 13th–18th; public admission from the 15th) in Berkeley Square is known for its lush mix of modern and contemporary design and art. Then walk over to the debut edition of London Invitational (October 15th–18th; public admission from the 16th) at the Chancery Rosewood hotel in Grosvenor Square. The wonderfully small fair brings together roughly a dozen galleries into the rarefied venue—formerly the U.S. Embassy, designed by Eero Saarinen. It’s a fitting setting for this new offshoot of the American fair Dallas Invitational. Then, hit the galleries. Three shows worth prioritizing: Louis Fratino at David Zwirner : Fratino’s first London solo show brings together new paintings of intimate domestic scenes and everyday life. Lucy Dodd at Sprüth Magers : New paintings made with peat, local herbs, copper ink, cochineal, and powdered meteorite draw on Artemis, the moon, and Dodd’s new surroundings in Scotland. Kylie Manning at Pace : For her first London solo show, Manning mixes London and Hampshire clay and Thames silt into her pigments, drawing on the city’s tradition of mudlarking—searching the riverbank for lost or rare objects. 4. Fair Play Oct. 15–18 | One Marylebone, 1 Marylebone Rd. | Marylebone One of the more intriguing newcomers to Frieze Week this year is Fair Play, a new artist-led fair in Marylebone. The model is what makes it especially interesting: Rather than galleries presenting booths, 70 artists selected by an independent committee will show and present their work directly, without paying to participate. It’s a chance to discover work beyond the traditional gallery system. It’s just south of Regent’s Park, making it an easy stop before or after Frieze. The fair’s invitation-only VIP day is on October 15th, and public admission opens the following day. 5. Somerset House Somerset House, Strand | Covent Garden There are several very good reasons to spend a half day, or maybe even the better part of a day, at Somerset House during Frieze Week. At the Courtauld, “ Salman Toor : Someone Like You” marks the artist’s first solo museum exhibition in Europe. The show brings together 19 paintings made since 2019, centered on love, friendship, and belonging. These tender, often emerald-hued worlds have made Toor one of the most beloved painters working today. Elsewhere in the complex, 1-54 Contemporary African Art Fair (October 15th–18th; public admission from the 16th) returns with galleries focused on contemporary art from Africa and its diaspora. This year’s edition places particular emphasis on African modernism. 6. Tate Modern Bankside, London SE1 9TG | Bankside A lot is happening at Tate Modern this week, but the newest attraction is in the Turbine Hall. Opening October 13th, the latest Hyundai Commission is by French-Lebanese artist Tarek Atoui , who works with sound and is known for inventing his own instruments. This new work builds on his long-running “I/E (Infinite Ears)” project, which explores how we experience sound. If you go on Friday or Saturday evening, from 7:00 to 8:30 p.m., Atoui will activate the installation through live performances with collaborators including Emptyset, mazen kerbaj , Kenichi Iwasa, and Aya Metwalli. Upstairs, the museum has multiple blockbuster exhibitions on view, which won’t be new to locals but may be to out-of-towners, including major shows of Ana Mendieta and Frida Kahlo . 7. Serpentine Galleries Kensington Gardens | Kensington I rarely need an excuse to wander through Hyde Park, but two compelling exhibitions at Serpentine make the trip especially worthwhile. At Serpentine South, Justin Caguiat presents “Change Ringing,” his first institutional exhibition in the U.K. Heat-responsive paintings shift with their environment, while bells sound throughout the galleries. Across the lake at Serpentine North, Amar Kanwar presents “The Charcoal Man,” a new seven-screen installation that brings together documentary, poetry, politics, and questions of violence and resistance. 8. National Portrait Gallery St. Martin’s Place | Westminster One of the exhibitions I’m most curious about this week is also one of the smallest. British painter Issy Wood inaugurates the National Portrait Gallery ’s new Artist Focus series with 12 self-portraits, shown together for the first time. Begun in 2020, the paintings offer a personal contrast to Wood’s better-known works, which typically feature uncanny objects, personalities, and interiors. It’s also free to see. Also recently opened is Tim Walker ’s exhibition “Fairyland: Love and Legends,” featuring some 250 portraits by the British photographer known for his fantastical approach to fashion photography. 9. The Barbican Barbican Centre, Silk St. | Barbican After several days of art fairs, if you’re ready to slow down and spend some time with serene Minimalism, this Robert Ryman show may be just what you need. “The Real Thing” brings together 60 works and marks the first major U.K. exhibition of Ryman’s paintings in more than 30 years. Ryman is best known for his white paintings, but the point was never simply the color. His work trains the eye on subtleties of surface, material, brushwork, scale, and even the way a painting touches the wall. The result is a calm, inquisitive show—and a welcome change of pace. 10. The National Gallery Trafalgar Square | Westminster For something completely different, head to the National Gallery for “Renoir and Love,” the first major U.K. survey of Pierre-Auguste Renoir since 2007. The show looks beyond romantic love to friendship and social life, bringing together major loans from collections around the world, including Bal du Moulin de la Galette (1876) from the Musée d’Orsay and Les grandes baigneuses (1884–87) from the Philadelphia Museum of Art . After a week navigating crowds looking at contemporary art, it might be nice to end among the lively crowds of 19th-century Paris. And if, like me, you’re heading to Paris next, consider it the perfect segue.
